content.text:
Mystery solved. The new code from #1145 is in your binary and a manifest IS on disk — but it was written from inside a **different worktree** (`.worktrees/redact`) than where you're running `--findings` (the main worktree). The loader at `manifest.go:236-238` strictly filters by `WorktreePath` equality, so manifests created in one worktree are invisible from another.

To see those findings, run `--findings` from the producing worktree:

```fish
cd /Users/peytonmontei/Documents/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/redact
entire review --findings
```

Or run a fresh `entire review` from the current main worktree to populate findings here.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Manifests live at `<git-common-dir>/entire-review/manifests/` — and `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` resolves to the same path from every linked worktree of the same repo. So a single shared directory holds manifests for all worktrees, but `loadLocalReviewManifests` (manifest.go:236) enforces a per-worktree visibility filter via `manifest.WorktreePath != worktreeRoot`. Deliberate scoping: each worktree sees only its own findings.
- This means the follow-up `entire review --fix <session-id>` line printed at the end of a review only resolves in the worktree where the review ran — moving terminals between the main checkout and `.worktrees/<name>` silently changes the visible result set, even though `.git/` is shared.
- A useful diagnostic when "where did my data go?" hits with anything under `.git/`: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` (current worktree) vs `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` (shared `.git/`). The mismatch is a strong hint that worktree-scoping logic is in play.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

I have enough to diagnose. Here's the chain.

**Why `entire review --findings` shows nothing**

`--findings` reads JSON manifests from `.git/entire-review/manifests/`. You have exactly **one** there — from a May 7 review that ran in `.worktrees/redact`, and the loader's per-worktree filter (`manifest.go:236`) hides it from the main worktree.

**Why your fresh review (12:36–12:52 today) didn't write a new manifest**

`writePostReviewManifest` (`cmd.go:637`) writes a manifest only if it can match each agent run to a session-state file with `Kind == "agent_review"`. The matcher in `manifest.go:104` discards sessions whose `Kind` is anything else — including null. The session JSONs for today's review (`8ad97f8d…` claude-code, `019e0872…` codex) were already cleaned up, but the surviving sessions on disk all show `"kind": null`, and the logs show **zero** "adopted review env" or "adoption skipped" entries during the 12:36–12:52 window. That means the lifecycle hook ran without `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION=1` in its environment — the silent early-return at `lifecycle.go:1042–1043`:

```go
if os.Getenv(review.EnvSession) != "1" {
    return  // no log
}
```

So the env-var handshake `entire review → claude -p → entire <hook>` is broken on your machine: env isn't reaching the hook subprocess. Three branches of `adoptReviewEnv` log on failure (agent mismatch / SHA mismatch / bad JSON); only the "env not set" branch is silent — and that's exactly what you hit. Likely cause is that `claude -p` (the argv `entire review` uses for claude-code, `reviewer.go:32`) is sanitizing or not propagating env to its hook child processes.

**Net effect:** every run silently no-ops the manifest write. `--findings` finds nothing, `--fix` has nothing to resolve.

**Quick way to confirm and unblock**

Run a review with file-level diagnostics, then check if the env actually reached the hook:

```fish
ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug entire review --agent codex
# in another tab while it runs
grep -E "adopted review|adoption skipped|review manifest" .entire/logs/entire.log | tail
```

Codex is a useful first probe because its launcher (`agent/codex/reviewer.go:39`) and Claude's are structurally identical, so if codex tags the session and claude doesn't, Claude's `-p` mode is the env-stripping culprit. If neither tags the session, the bug is upstream of the agent fork (e.g., the spawn path itself isn't running the AgentReviewer with `cmd.Env` populated).

Either way, the fix likely belongs in #1145's adoption path — adding a more useful "EnvSession unset" debug log would have made this self-diagnosable, and falling back to a checkpoint-id/process-id heuristic in `writePostReviewManifest` when `Kind` matching turns up empty would make the feature degrade gracefully instead of silently producing nothing.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The env-var handshake design is elegant when it works: each spawned agent gets its own `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` env, so multi-tenant correctness is "by construction" with no shared marker file (CLAUDE.md anti-features explicitly bans the older marker-file approach). But it has one fragility this codebase didn't account for: it assumes every agent CLI propagates env to its hook subprocesses unmodified. When a CLI does anything cute with env (whitelist filtering, scrubbing for cache-key stability, `-p` short-circuit paths), the entire feature silently no-ops.
- The "silent failure" in `adoptReviewEnv` line 1042 is exactly the kind of pattern `superpowers:silent-failure-hunter` exists to catch — every other branch logs at WARN, but the most-common-in-practice failure mode logs nothing. That's why this issue is so opaque from the outside: there's no error, no warning, no missing-file message — just an empty `--findings` list with no breadcrumbs.
- A useful debugging shortcut for "env vars not reaching child" bugs in agent CLIs: `strace -f -e trace=execve` (Linux) or `dtruss -f` (macOS) on `entire review` will show every `execve` in the tree along with its argv AND envp, making it obvious where in the parent→agent→hook chain the variable disappears. Cheaper than instrumenting the code.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

`Sources` is built only from session-state files where `Kind == "agent_review"` (`manifest.go:104`). Since the env-var handshake never tagged today's review sessions (the `os.Getenv("ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION") != "1"` silent return in `lifecycle.go:1042`), `Sources` is empty, the manifest write skips, **and** the footer skips. The missing `--fix` hint and the empty `--findings` list are the same symptom of the same bug.

So: one broken upstream (env propagation from `entire review` → agent CLI → hook subprocess), three downstream features that all silently no-op (manifest persistence, `--findings` browsing, end-of-run footer hint). Nothing in the user-visible review output ever announces the failure — exactly the silent-failure pattern this codebase's own anti-features list and `superpowers:silent-failure-hunter` agent are designed to catch.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This is a textbook case of a "feature trio with one shared dependency" failing as a unit. The author bundled manifest write, footer print, and findings list all behind `Kind == "agent_review"` filtering — sensible factoring, but it means a single upstream regression silently kills three user-visible features at once. A defensive design would have decoupled the footer (print whenever ≥1 agent succeeded) from manifest persistence (gate on `Kind` match if you must), so at minimum the user gets the next-step nudge even if the manifest can't be persisted.
- The `lifecycle.go:1042` silent return is the bridge between the visible bug (no footer, no findings) and the invisible cause (env not propagating). That single line is the highest-leverage fix in the whole feature: changing it to log "review env not detected at hook time" at INFO would have made this a 30-second diagnosis instead of an hour of code spelunking. Worth filing as the smallest possible follow-up PR independent of the broader env-propagation fix.
- Worth checking whether your local `claude` CLI version is sanitizing env for hooks — Anthropic's `claude` has historically had a hook-env passthrough policy that varied between versions; if a recent claude release tightened that, every `entire review` user gets this bug regardless of CLI version, which would explain why a feature that shipped in #1145 with passing tests now no-ops in the wild.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

content.text:
Three converging causes — none of them caught the bug because each one sits in a blind spot of the next.

**1. The test pyramid never exercised real env propagation.**

Every test stubs out the chain at a different layer:

- `reviewer_test.go:40-62` checks `cmd.Env` on the unexecuted `*exec.Cmd` — verifies the env was set, never runs anything.
- `lifecycle_test.go:1298+` uses `t.Setenv(...)` to put the vars in the *test process's* env, then calls `adoptReviewEnv` directly — verifies the function reads env correctly, never goes through a subprocess.
- `integration_test/review_test.go:41-50` builds a synthetic `reviewEnv` slice and hands it to `SimulateUserPromptSubmitWithReviewEnvVars` — verifies the adoption pipeline if the env is present, never tests that it gets there.
- The Vogon canary (`e2e/vogon/`) doesn't cover the `--findings`/`--fix`/footer code path at all.
- Real-agent E2E tests are gated behind `mise run test:e2e` and aren't part of `test:ci`, so they don't block merges.

The PR's verification block (`go test ./cmd/entire/cli/review ./cmd/entire/cli ./cmd/entire/cli/settings`) ran exactly these green-but-blind tests. So "all tests pass" gave full confidence in a propagation chain whose middle link was never executed.

**2. The design assumed a property that doesn't always hold.**

`AppendReviewEnv` (`env.go:94`) and `adoptReviewEnv` (`lifecycle.go:1037`) form a contract: parent sets env on agent process, agent inherits, agent's hook subprocess inherits transitively. That works *if* the agent CLI passes its own env to hook subprocesses verbatim. Claude Code in `-p` (one-shot) mode is the most likely violator — `claude -p` is the argv `entire review` uses for claude-code (`reviewer.go:32`), and `-p` mode has historically had different lifecycle semantics than interactive mode. Other launchable agents (codex, gemini-cli) plausibly behave the same way or differently; the design treated them all uniformly. The CLAUDE.md anti-features section even brags about ditching the older marker-file approach in favor of "multi-tenant correctness by construction" — that's correct *given* the propagation assumption, but the assumption itself was never validated.

**3. The failure mode collapses three signals into one silent return.**

`lifecycle.go:1042-1043`:

```go
if os.Getenv(review.EnvSession) != "1" {
    return  // no log
}
```

This branch fires for two semantically different cases:
- **Normal session** — silence is correct (don't spam logs for every non-review turn).
- **Review session whose env was stripped** — silence hides the bug.

The hook can't distinguish them from inside, because the only signal that "this *should* be a review" is the env var that just went missing. So the bug presents identically to normal operation: no error, no warning, no missing-file message. Then three downstream features (manifest persistence, `--findings`, end-of-run footer) all gate on the same `Kind == "agent_review"` check at `manifest.go:104`, so a single silent miss kills them as a unit.

**Net causal story:** PR #1145 replaced a marker-file design (which would have shown a stale or missing file diagnostically) with an env-var design (which fails invisibly when env is stripped); the test suite never executed the propagation chain end-to-end; the failure handler treats "env missing" as the no-op default; and three user-visible features were factored to share that single silently-failing check. Each of those choices is locally reasonable; together they produce a feature that ships green and silently no-ops in production.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The deeper lesson is about **test coverage at the boundary you actually care about**. The PR has unit tests on both *sides* of the env handshake (sender sets env correctly; receiver reads env correctly) but no test of the wire between them. This is a recurring pattern in subprocess-mediated features — and the only reliable defense is a test that actually forks the real CLI and inspects the resulting subprocess env (e.g., a tiny "echo my env" agent in `e2e/vogon/` that prints `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` to stderr, which the test scrapes). A 15-line addition to the canary would have caught this on the merging PR.
- The marker-file → env-var migration was sold as a fix for a multi-tenant correctness problem (concurrent worktrees racing on a shared file). But the new design just trades one class of bugs for another: marker files have visible, debuggable state; env vars have invisible, ephemeral state that vanishes the moment a subprocess fork doesn't cooperate. Both have legitimate failure modes — the question is which failure mode you can *detect*. A hybrid (env-var primary, marker-file fallback at agent-spawn time so the hook can probe both) is uglier but bulletproof, and would have given today's symptom an immediately legible diagnosis.
- Worth noting that this codebase already has a `superpowers:silent-failure-hunter` agent specifically calibrated to flag exactly this `if cond { return }` pattern in code review. If it had been run against #1145's diff at PR time, the silent return at `lifecycle.go:1042` is exactly the kind of construct it would have surfaced — combined with the matcher's silent skip at `manifest.go:104` and the manifest write's silent early returns at `cmd.go:645/653`, that's *four* silent failure points stacked in a row, none of which log anything an operator can grep for. Running the silent-failure-hunter on review-related diffs going forward would catch the next instance of this class.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Fair pushback — I was too sure too fast. Here's what's actually different:

**The May 7 manifest was written 2 hours BEFORE #1145 merged to main** (manifest at 19:55 UTC; merge at 21:47 UTC). Which means: the user wrote it from a checkout of the feature branch in `.worktrees/redact`, almost certainly while testing the PR. That run worked. Today's run on main, with the same code (now merged), didn't. So the code paths are identical — what changed is the *runtime environment* the review is running inside.

Look at this log line from today's review:

```
"session_id":"6a33efd5-..."   ← ambient logging context
"event":"SessionStart"
"session_id":"8ad97f8d-..."   ← the actual review session
```

The session_id appears twice. The outer one (`6a33efd5`) is your daytime ambient claude-code session — running since 11:03 today. The inner one (`8ad97f8d`) is the review. So `entire review` wasn't run from a fresh terminal — it was run from *inside* an outer claude session, almost certainly via the Bash tool.

That changes the env-propagation chain meaningfully:

```
fresh terminal:   fish → entire review → claude -p  → entire <hook>
                                          ↑ env set here, inherited cleanly

via outer claude: outer-claude → Bash tool → entire review → claude -p → entire <hook>
                                  ↑ env may be filtered/sanitized here ↑ may inherit a DIFFERENT outer env
```

Claude Code's Bash tool is known to sanitize/restrict env when shelling out (it's documented to drop interactive-shell vars and to set its own `CLAUDE_*` markers), and either of two things could break the handshake:

1. The Bash tool's sandboxed env doesn't include something that `paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)` or `git rev-parse HEAD` needs, so `cfg.StartingSHA` ends up empty in the env, the hook's `EnvStartingSHA != state.BaseCommit` check fires (`lifecycle.go:1052`), and adoption is skipped — but with a *log* this time. Worth grepping for.
2. The inner `claude -p` is spawned with `cmd.Env = AppendReviewEnv(os.Environ(), ...)`, where `os.Environ()` is the entire-review process's own env. If the outer claude's Bash tool injected `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` vars from some prior contaminated state (e.g., a leaked review env that should have been stripped), `AppendReviewEnv` strips them (env.go:97-101) and re-adds the right ones — that path is safe. So this isn't it.

The real test: was today's run from your terminal directly, or did Claude (in this very conversation, or earlier) shell out via Bash to do it for you? If the latter, you've found the regression: **#1145 only works when invoked from an environment that propagates env cleanly, and the Bash-tool path doesn't.** That's not "feature broken" — that's "feature has an unstated precondition that the test suite never exercised."

Yes, fix it. The reason is exactly what you're pointing at — "new terminal" being the difference is a *symptom*, not an explanation, and a feature whose correctness depends on which terminal you launched it from is broken even when it appears to work.

What "new terminal" actually rules out

Your old shell had something in its environment that the new one didn't. Two candidates account for almost all "works in fresh shell" cases:

1. **Stale `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` from a prior aborted run** — if you ever exported these manually for debugging, or a previous `entire review` left them set in your shell (it shouldn't, but a crashed parent could), `os.Environ()` in the new run picks them up. `AppendReviewEnv` (env.go:97-101) tries to defend against this by stripping pre-existing `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` keys before re-adding them, so this path *should* be safe — but only for those specific keys.

2. **Ambient state from a parent agent process** — your old terminal was inside or downstream of an active claude-code session (likely `6a33efd5`, which the logs show was alive all day). When that session shells out, it injects its own `CLAUDE_*` markers and may filter or replace env. If anything in that chain dropped or rewrote a var the spawn path needed (PATH, HOME, GIT_*), `paths.WorktreeRoot(ctx)` or `git rev-parse HEAD` inside `entire review` would resolve differently than they do in your new terminal — and `cfg.StartingSHA` would end up empty or wrong, blowing the SHA check at `lifecycle.go:1052` silently.

You can identify which one by running this in your *old* terminal (don't open a new one first):

```fish
env | grep -E '^(ENTIRE_|CLAUDE_|GIT_|PATH=|HOME=|PWD=)' | sort
```

Compare to the same command in a fresh terminal. The diff is the proximate cause.

Why this needs fixing regardless

The bug isn't "stale env in shell" — that's a user-state issue. The bug is that **the failure mode is invisible**. Three small fixes would make this self-diagnosing instead of "open an issue and pray someone reproduces it":

1. **lifecycle.go:1042** — replace the silent return with a debug log: `logging.Debug(ctx, "review env adoption skipped: ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION not set", ...)`. Five lines. Today's whole hour-long debugging session collapses to one grep.

2. **cmd.go:653** — when `manifest.Sources == 0`, print a *user-visible* warning to stderr (not just debug log): `"warning: review completed but session was not tagged as a review; --findings will not see this run. Run with ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug to diagnose."` That single line means the next user hits the same bug and can self-help instead of opening "feature doesn't work" with no logs.

3. **`AppendReviewEnv` is too narrow** — it strips stale `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` but doesn't probe whether the env actually arrives at the hook. A simple defense: have `entire review` write a sentinel file at `<git-common-dir>/entire-review/.handshake-<run-id>` containing `{run_id, starting_sha, agent}`, set `ENTIRE_REVIEW_RUN=<run-id>` on the spawned agent, and at hook time look up the sentinel by run-id env var. If the env var arrived → use the env path. If not → fall back to "look for any sentinel younger than this hook's SessionStart that names this agent." Belt-and-suspenders, costs ~30 lines, and the marker file is debuggable when env propagation fails (you can `cat` it and see exactly what the parent set).

The CLAUDE.md anti-features list explicitly bans the `PendingReviewMarker` for launchable agents because the env-var design "makes it unnecessary." That was true on a clean process tree. It's not true under nested agent invocations. The marker isn't a regression — it's a fallback for when the elegant primary path can't deliver.

If you want to file these, fix #1 alone is high-leverage and tiny. #2 prevents the silent-failure UX you just hit. #3 is bigger and worth a brainstorm on whether the marker fallback for non-launchable agents could be reused as a defense-in-depth for launchable ones too.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- "Works in a fresh terminal" is a load-bearing diagnostic clue for env-propagation bugs, but it's also a tell that the feature has an undeclared precondition: *the ambient environment must be clean*. Features should declare their preconditions in code (validate, fail loudly) or eliminate the dependency on them. Silently degrading when a precondition isn't met is the worst outcome — the feature appears to run, costs full agent tokens, and produces nothing.
- The fact that #1145's tests all pass but the feature breaks under realistic invocation is a useful generalization: when a feature's contract spans process boundaries, *unit tests on either side of the boundary are insufficient by construction* — only end-to-end tests that actually fork the boundary can verify it. A 30-line addition to the Vogon canary that runs `entire review --agent vogon` and asserts a manifest appears would have caught this on the merging PR. Cheap insurance.
- The "elegant primary, ugly fallback" pattern (env var primary, marker file fallback) is uncomfortable but correct for cross-process contracts. It mirrors how TCP works (clean connection state primary, RST/timeout fallback) — you can't ship a real-world feature that only works when the network is perfect, and you can't ship a real-world feature that only works when env propagation is perfect. The CLAUDE.md anti-features section is sound design advice for the happy path; it's wrong about the unhappy path.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

That filter was narrow though (only `ENTIRE_`/`CLAUDE_`/`GIT_`/`PATH`/`HOME`/`PWD`). The actual difference, if it's in env at all, is something else. Worth one more diff:

```fish

If that diff is empty, env wasn't the culprit at all and the difference is somewhere else in the process state — most likely the **process tree**: was your "old" terminal a tab inside a tmux/zellij/iTerm session that itself was launched by an outer claude/codex/agent process? `ps -o pid,ppid,command -p $$` in each shell will show the parent PID and the `pstree`-style ancestry will tell you immediately.

But here's the practical bottom line on your real question — **do we still need to fix?**

Yes, unconditionally. The reason is independent of the root cause:

The feature has at least one invocation context where it silently no-ops, costs full agent tokens, and produces nothing the user can act on. That's true whether the trigger is env pollution, process-tree nesting, a claude-code `-p` mode quirk, or something we haven't identified. Even if you never reproduce the original failure, the next person hitting any of these contexts hits the same dead-silent failure mode with no logs and no error message.

The fix doesn't require pinning down which silent return fired — it requires making *all* the silent returns visible:

1. **`lifecycle.go:1042`** — log at debug when adoption is skipped because env is missing. (5 lines)
2. **`cmd.go:653`** — print a stderr warning to the user when `manifest.Sources == 0`: "review completed but session was not tagged; --findings will not see this run." (3 lines)
3. **`cmd.go:407` and `cmd.go:552`** — after `writePostReviewManifest` returns, the parent has full visibility into whether a manifest was written. If it wasn't, surface that in the user-visible review summary, not just debug logs.

With those three changes in place, the next reproduction tells you the root cause in one log grep. Without them, every future user who hits this — for whatever reason — opens "review --findings doesn't work" with the same opaque story you just walked through.

So: file the silent-failure fixes regardless. The root-cause investigation can continue in parallel and may or may not converge — but the silent failure is a known bug with a known cheap fix, and shipping it gates being able to diagnose anything else in this code path.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This investigation is a textbook case for the principle that **observability fixes ship before root-cause fixes**. We've spent this whole conversation reverse-engineering process state from after-the-fact log grepping precisely because the code doesn't emit the breadcrumbs we'd need to diagnose live. Three log lines added at PR-time would have made today's hour-long thread a 30-second answer. When you find a silent failure, the first patch is *making it loud*, not fixing it — because making it loud is what lets you fix it correctly.
- The env-diff being empty (so far) is interesting evidence in its own right: it suggests the propagation problem may not be at the *shell* level but deeper in the process tree. macOS Terminal apps inherit a frozen snapshot of env at app launch time, but anything launched inside a tmux/zellij multiplexer inherits the multiplexer's env, which can differ significantly from what `env` shows in a child shell. If your "broken" terminal was a tmux pane attached from earlier in the day and the "working" one was a fresh window, that alone could explain the difference without anything you'd see in `env`.
- Filing this as a single PR (logging + user-visible warning, stacked on top of the existing review feature) is exactly the kind of small, mergeable improvement that's worth doing immediately — it's contained, doesn't change behavior on the happy path, and pays for itself the first time someone else hits the silent-failure mode. Holding it back to bundle with a "real fix" delays the diagnostic capability that *finds* the real fix.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

That eliminates every theory I had about shell-level state. The difference must be one of:

- **Process tree** — ppid/grandparent of your shell. Run `ps -o pid,ppid,command -p $$` in each (if the old terminal is still alive) and `ps -p $PPID` walking up. If old terminal's ancestry includes a `claude` or `codex` or other agent process that the new one's doesn't, that's it.
- **Concurrent state on disk** — at 12:36 you had multiple sessions live (the ambient `6a33efd5` was running since 11:03, plus the review's two). State-store locking, transcript flush timing, or a checkpoint-write race could have produced the silent miss. Less reproducible, harder to diagnose, but real.
- **Transient agent CLI state** — claude-code or codex may have had a stale session cache, hung subprocess, etc., that's since cleared. Untestable after the fact.

Here's the better forcing function — you've now got a *working* run from a fresh terminal. Verify it actually produced what we expect, and look at what its logs say:

```fish
# Did the working run land a new manifest?
ls -lt .git/entire-review/manifests/ | head -3

# What did adoption actually do during the working run?
grep -E "adopted review env|adoption skipped|review env adoption|review manifest" .entire/logs/entire.log | tail -20
```

If the working run produced a manifest *and* the log shows `"adopted review env"` — we have a clean reference for what the failing run should have logged. Then a `grep` of the failing run's window (12:36–12:52) for those same messages tells us exactly which branch fired (or didn't).

If the working run produced a manifest with *no* adoption log line either — then env adoption isn't logging at all even on success, and my read of the debug logs is wrong somewhere.

Either way: paste the output of those two commands and we can pin it down.

But — and I want to be clear about this — **don't gate filing the fixes on root-causing.** You've already established:
- The feature silently no-ops in at least one realistic invocation context.
- The failure produces no error, no warning, no missing file the user can find.
- The user-visible behavior is identical to "feature works fine, no findings yet."

That's enough to merit a small PR with the three logging/warning improvements I described. They're independent of root cause, they're cheap, and they're what makes the next reproduction debuggable. Root-cause investigation can continue with proper instrumentation in place.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The honest meta-lesson here: I confidently produced three theories (env stripping, stale env contamination, nested-claude Bash tool), each one ruled out by the next data point. That's not a failure of reasoning — that's the normal shape of debugging a silent failure with insufficient logs. But it's worth naming explicitly: every confident theory I gave you was a *speculation dressed as a diagnosis*, and the only thing that disproved each one was new data you went out and collected. When an AI assistant gives you a confident root-cause story without proposing a verification step, push back the way you did. "How do I test it?" was the right question and it cut through three layers of plausible-but-unverified theorizing in two terminal commands.
- The empty env diff is itself diagnostic information, not a dead end. It tells you the bug is *deeper than shell state*, which narrows the search dramatically. Many real bugs hide in process-tree inheritance (env at fork time, not at shell-export time), open file descriptors, controlling terminals, or kernel-level process state that no `env` command surfaces. macOS in particular is hostile to introspecting process trees post-hoc — `pstree` is non-standard, `ps` lineage walking is manual, and Activity Monitor flattens parent-child relationships. If you find yourself debugging "works in a fresh terminal" issues regularly, `brew install pstree` is worth the 10 seconds.
- Worth noting that the user-visible *symptom* (no footer, no findings) and the *root cause* (some specific process-state difference) are at very different abstraction levels. The fix at the symptom level (always print SOMETHING when review completes, even if it's "manifest not written, see logs") is independently valuable and far easier to ship than the root-cause fix. Production code should optimize for "is failure visible?" first, "is failure rare?" second. We've been backwards on that here.

func writePostReviewManifest(ctx context.Context, out io.Writer, ...) {
    if summary.Cancelled || len(summary.AgentRuns) == 0 {
        return  // legitimate — nothing to persist
    }
    manifest, err := localReviewManifestFromCurrentState(...)
    if err != nil {
        logging.Debug(ctx, "review manifest not written", slog.String("error", err.Error()))
        warnManifestNotWritten(out, "could not load session state: "+err.Error())

        warnManifestNotWritten(out, "review session was not tagged as a review (env-var handshake did not reach the hook)")
        return
    }
    if err := writeLocalReviewManifest(ctx, manifest); err != nil {
        logging.Debug(ctx, "review manifest write failed", slog.String("error", err.Error()))
        warnManifestNotWritten(out, "write to disk failed: "+err.Error())
        return

func warnManifestNotWritten(out io.Writer, reason string) {
    fmt.Fprintln(out)

For 99% of users, **nothing changes**. The fix is invisible on the happy path — successful reviews look identical to how they look today.

The change is only visible when something silently fails. Concretely:

**Today, when the manifest write skips (your 12:36 case):**

```
codex                 ✓ done      7m40s

2 agent(s) done — 2 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 cancelled
Generating summary...

  ## Unified Review Verdict
  ...

[end of output — that's it]
```

You see the review output, the synthesis, and then nothing. No error, no warning, no hint that anything went wrong. You only discover the failure later when `entire review --findings` says nothing's there.

**After the fix, same scenario:**

```
codex                 ✓ done      7m40s

2 agent(s) done — 2 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 cancelled
Generating summary...

  ## Unified Review Verdict
  ...

Note: review skills ran successfully but findings were not persisted.
  Reason: review session was not tagged as a review (env-var handshake did not reach the hook)
  `entire review --findings` and `entire review --fix` will not see this run.
  Re-run with `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug` for diagnostic detail.
```

Same agent output, same synthesis — but instead of trailing off into nothing, the user gets four lines telling them exactly what happened, what won't work as a result, and how to dig deeper.

**On the happy path (today's working case from a fresh terminal):**

Nothing changes. The "Review complete. To apply all review findings: ..." footer prints exactly as it does now. The only difference is that the code path leading up to it has one extra branch that *would* print the warning if `Sources == 0`, but on a working run that branch never fires.

**Debug log change (lifecycle.go:1042):**

Invisible to users entirely unless they explicitly set `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. Even then it only adds one line per non-review turn to the log file (which lives at `.entire/logs/`). Users running normally never see it.

So the user-visible surface is exactly: *one warning block in the failure case, zero changes on the happy path*. That's the whole UX delta. The rest of the PR (debug logs, helper function, tests) is plumbing that makes the failure case diagnosable but doesn't change what users see.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- This is the right shape for a silent-failure fix: zero noise added to the success path, useful information added to the failure path. The mistake to avoid is the opposite shape — adding "for your information" output to the happy path "in case something goes wrong," which is what produces the dreaded warning-spam-everyone-ignores problem. The user should never see new output unless something actually failed.
- The exact wording of the warning matters more than its existence. "Reason: review session was not tagged as a review (env-var handshake did not reach the hook)" is jargon-heavy and assumes context the user doesn't have. Real-world v2 of this would probably soften it: "Reason: a setup step didn't complete; agents ran but their output won't be retrievable later." Less precise, but understandable to the median user. Worth iterating on copy with someone less in-the-weeds than us — e.g., paste both versions to a coworker who didn't follow this thread and see which one actually communicates.
- One thing notably absent from this PR: any attempt to recover. The warning tells the user "this run won't be visible to --findings" but doesn't offer to retry, save the agent output to a file as a consolation prize, or let them attach the run via `entire review attach <session-id>`. There's a reasonable v2 conversation about whether the warning should also write the agent narratives to a fallback file (`.git/entire-review/orphans/<timestamp>.txt`) so the work isn't fully lost. But that adds complexity, and the v1 fix should ship first — recovery is a separate design question.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
but this only shows up if it doesn't get tagged as review session so then when it works properly everything looks normal?

Correct. On a working review, the warning never fires — output is identical to today. The user sees the same agent narratives, the same synthesis verdict, the same "Review complete. To apply all review findings: ..." footer. No new lines, no new prompts, no behavioral changes.

The warning is strictly a failure-path feature. It fires only when one of three things goes wrong inside `writePostReviewManifest`:

1. Loading session state from disk fails (system error)
2. Sessions exist but none are tagged as reviews (today's bug — handshake didn't take)
3. Writing the manifest file fails (disk full, permissions, etc.)

All three are silent today. All three become visible after this fix. None of them happen on a normal working run.

So the change is asymmetric on purpose: zero noise added when things work, useful guidance added when they don't. That's the entire UX delta.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The good shape of this fix is what makes it mergeable on its own merits. Reviewers can convince themselves quickly that it can't regress the happy path — every new line of output is gated behind an existing failure check that today already returns silently. There's no scenario where this change makes a working review noisier or behave differently. That property (zero risk to the success path) is what lets observability fixes ship fast, ahead of the riskier root-cause work.
- The asymmetry — silence on success, signal on failure — is also what distinguishes a *good* warning from a *spammy* one. Many codebases accumulate warnings that print on every invocation "just in case," and users learn to tune them out. A warning that only fires when the stated invariant has actually been violated retains its signal value. Users who never hit the bug never see the warning; users who hit it learn from it.
- Worth noting that even after this fix lands, the **debug log line at `lifecycle.go:1042`** is the more powerful diagnostic artifact for engineers. The user-visible warning answers "did my run work?" — which is what users care about. The debug log answers "*why* didn't it work?" — which is what the next bug-fixing engineer needs. Both are valuable; they serve different audiences. PR descriptions for observability fixes should make that distinction explicit so reviewers don't ask "why are we logging the same thing twice?" — they're not, they're capturing different facts for different readers.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

A 30-second eyeball of real output catches things tests will never catch (visual layout, copy clarity, ordering surprises) and is the appropriate complement to automated coverage rather than a replacement for it.

gh pr create --title "feat(review): warn user when review manifest is not persisted" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

- Silent-failure observability fix for `entire review`: when manifest persistence skips (env-handshake didn't reach the hook, state-store load fails, or disk write fails), the user now sees a clear note explaining what happened and how to diagnose.
- Adds a debug log on the previously-silent `EnvSession`-not-set return in `adoptReviewEnv`, completing observability across all five adoption decisions.
- Happy path is unchanged: successful reviews print identical output.

## Background

After running `entire review`, three downstream features (`entire review --findings`, `entire review --fix`, and the end-of-run "To apply all review findings:" footer) all read from the local manifest at `.git/entire-review/manifests/`. If the spawned agent's lifecycle hook does not adopt the `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` env vars set by `entire review` — for any reason — the session is never tagged as `KindAgentReview`, the manifest matcher finds zero sources, and `writePostReviewManifest` returns silently. All three features then quietly no-op with no error, no warning, no missing-file message that a user could grep.

We hit this in practice today: a review ran end-to-end, agents produced findings, the synthesis verdict printed — and then `entire review --findings` claimed there was nothing to show, with no breadcrumb in the user-visible output explaining why. The actual root cause for that specific reproduction is still unidentified (running from a fresh terminal worked; running from the same shell a few hours earlier did not, with identical shell env). Without observability in the failure path, every future reproduction will be equally opaque.

## What this PR does

**`cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go`** — Two-line debug log added to the `EnvSession`-not-set silent return. The other four branches in `adoptReviewEnv` already log at WARN (agent mismatch, SHA mismatch, malformed skills JSON) or DEBUG (success). This was the only branch with no breadcrumb, so a "review env didn't take" failure produced zero log lines diagnosing it.

**`cmd/entire/cli/review/cmd.go`** — Each of the three silent early returns in `writePostReviewManifest` now also calls a new helper `warnManifestNotWritten` which prints a user-visible four-line note to the same `out` writer the success-path footer uses. The helper is centralized so the wording is consistent and editable in one place.

## What this PR does NOT do

- Does not attempt to fix the root-cause env-propagation problem. The conditions under which the handshake breaks are not yet reliably reproducible. This PR makes the *next* reproduction debuggable in 30 seconds (one log grep) instead of an hour (reverse-engineering process state from logs).
- Does not change behavior on the happy path. Working reviews print the same output they do today.
- Does not touch the matcher logic, spawn path, or contract between agents and hooks.

## User-visible change

**Today, when manifest persistence skips:**
```
2 agent(s) done — 2 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 cancelled
Generating summary...
[synthesis output]

[end of output — no error, no warning, no signal that --findings won't see this run]
```

**After this PR, same scenario:**
```
2 agent(s) done — 2 succeeded, 0 failed, 0 cancelled
Generating summary...
[synthesis output]

Note: review skills ran successfully but findings were not persisted.
  Reason: review session was not tagged as a review (env-var handshake did not reach the hook)
  `entire review --findings` and `entire review --fix` will not see this run.
  Re-run with `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug` for diagnostic detail.
```

## Test plan

- [x] `mise run fmt` clean
- [x] `mise run lint` — 0 issues
- [x] `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/review/` passes (incl. two new tests: `TestWarnManifestNotWritten_PrintsReasonAndDiagnosticHints`, `TestWritePostReviewManifest_WarnsWhenNoMatchingSessions`)
- [x] `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/` passes
- [x] `mise run test:integration` passes (incl. existing `TestReview_EnvVarAdoptionCondensesReviewMetadataOnNextCommit` — confirms happy-path env adoption still works)
- [x] Manual smoke test: real `entire review --agent codex` from a fresh terminal on this branch successfully writes a manifest and prints the existing "Review complete." footer with `--fix <id>` commands. Warning correctly does **not** fire on success.

## Decisions worth flagging for review

- **Debug-level (not WARN) for the new lifecycle log.** This branch fires on every normal coding turn (any session that isn't a review), so logging at WARN/INFO would flood the operator's log with one line per user prompt. DEBUG keeps it silent unless someone explicitly opts in via `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug`.
- **No log-capture test for the new lifecycle log line.** The logging package's package-level singleton makes log assertions heavy. The existing behavioral test (`TestAdoptReviewEnv_NormalSession`) covers the path; if the log line is ever removed, behavior is unchanged but observability degrades silently. Acceptable risk for v1; revisit if a future reproduction shows this matters.
- **Wording of the failure note.** The "env-var handshake did not reach the hook" phrasing is precise but jargony. Open to wording suggestions from review.

content.text:
Both Copilot comments addressed in commit `00fc0eb4b`:

| Comment | Fix |
|---|---|
| Log "not set" inaccurate when value is not `"1"` | Reworded to `"ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION is not \"1\""` + added `observed_value` slog field |
| Warning says "ran successfully" but agents may have failed | Dropped "successfully" — per-agent statuses already shown earlier in output |

Verification:
- `mise run fmt` clean
- `mise run lint` — 0 issues
- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/review/` — passing
- Pushed to PR #1166

Both changes are minimal and address exactly what the reviewer flagged. The user-visible warning now reads:

```
Note: review skills ran but findings were not persisted.
  Reason: review session was not tagged as a review (env-var handshake did not reach the hook)
  `entire review --findings` and `entire review --fix` will not see this run.
  Re-run with `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug` for diagnostic detail.
```

The debug log on the silent skip now includes the observed value, so a future failure with `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION=0` (e.g., from a wrapper script that's setting it wrong) is immediately distinguishable in logs from `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION` being unset entirely.

The Copilot review thread on GitHub stays "unresolved" until manually marked — that's a click on the GitHub UI, not something `gh` can do reliably for bot reviews. If you want me to leave a reply on the inline thread referencing the fix commit so it's clear the feedback was addressed, I can do that via `gh api`. Otherwise the new commit speaks for itself.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Both Copilot comments pointed at real problems with my wording precision. The "not set" → "is not '1'" fix is a subtle correctness issue: it would mislead a future debugger reading logs in the `ENTIRE_REVIEW_SESSION=0` case, sending them to look for "missing env" when really the env was set to a wrong value. That's the exact category of error the PR is designed to *prevent* — opaque log messages that send debuggers down the wrong path. Fixing it brought the PR into alignment with its own thesis.
- Including the observed value as a structured slog field (`observed_value`) rather than baking it into the message string is the right pattern: structured fields are queryable, unique-per-call, and preserved through log shipping pipelines. Putting it in the message would have given `slog` a high-cardinality message string that defeats log aggregation. Worth a default habit: when a log line names a condition, name the *abstract* condition in the message and put the *concrete* values in fields.
- The "ran successfully" wording fix is interesting because it's a case where you have to reason about reachability — *which combinations of `summary.Cancelled`, `len(AgentRuns)`, and per-agent `Status` actually reach this code?* — to know what claims are safe. It's exactly the kind of detail a human reviewer might miss but that a bot reviewer (which actually reads the early-return chain) catches reliably. PR review bots earning their keep.

All four are real bugs, all separate from the current PR, all worth filing. Quick characterization of each:

**1. Agent failure has no surfaced reason**

When an agent process fails (non-zero exit, parser scanner.Err, RunError event), the user sees `✗ failed` in the dashboard and a final tally line — but the actual stderr/error message gets swallowed somewhere between the agent process and the user. Likely culprits: the parser (`parseClaudeOutput`/`parseCodexOutput`) emits `RunError{Err: ...}` but neither `TUISink` nor `DumpSink` may render the error text prominently in the failure case. Worth tracing one error event end-to-end through the sink chain.

**2. Tokens column always empty**

The `TOKENS` column is fed by `AgentRun.Tokens`, which is populated by `TokensUpdate` events from each parser. If Claude's `-p` mode and Codex's stdout don't emit token counts in a format the parsers recognize (or if the parsers don't have `TokensUpdate` emission at all), the column stays empty for every run. Quick check: `grep TokensUpdate cmd/entire/cli/agent/*/reviewer.go` — if the result is empty or only emits zero tokens, that's the whole bug.

**3. Ctrl+O drill-in is unhelpful**

Two distinct problems wrapped together:
- During the run: drill-in shows event buffer but live output isn't tailed/scrollable
- For long output: doesn't paginate or scroll, just truncates

`tui_detail.go` is where this lives. Likely missing `viewport.Model` from bubbles for scrolling, and probably doesn't auto-scroll on append.

**4. Codex reviewed against wrong branch (`issues...HEAD` instead of `main...HEAD`)**

This is the highest-impact one. Confirmed by reading `scope.go:122-205`: `detectScopeBaseRef` picks the merged-into-HEAD branch with the **most-recent tip timestamp** as the scope base. If you have any branch (`issues`, an old feature branch, a stale local) whose tip commit timestamp is newer than `main`'s, that branch wins — regardless of whether it's actually the branch you want to review against. The doc comment frames this as "stacked PR support" (prefer immediate parent over main), but in practice it picks unintended bases very easily.

The fallback chain (`origin/HEAD → origin/main → origin/master → main → master`) only fires when **no** ancestor branches exist, which is rare. So the smart-but-fragile timestamp heuristic dominates in practice.

This bug fires on **every review run with stale local branches in the repo**. It's wasting agent tokens reviewing the wrong scope, every time. Plausibly the highest-leverage bug of the four.

The fix is a design question, not a code question:
- Option A: invert the priority — `origin/main` first, fall back to "closest ancestor" only when explicitly opted in.
- Option B: add a `--base <ref>` flag so users can override.
- Option C: detect the typical "PR target" via `gh pr view --json baseRefName` if `gh` is available; fall back to `origin/main`.
- Option D: keep current heuristic but require the picked base to also be reachable from `origin/main` (i.e., must be an ancestor of mainline).

Each has tradeoffs. Worth a brainstorm before any code.

**Recommendation**

File these as four separate GitHub issues:

| # | Issue | Severity | Fix size |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agent failure errors not surfaced to user | High | Small (1–2 files, sink rendering) |
| 2 | Tokens column always empty | Medium | Small if parser missing emit; medium if parser exists but agent output doesn't include tokens |
| 3 | Ctrl+O drill-in lacks scrolling/live tail | Medium | Medium (viewport refactor in `tui_detail.go`) |
| 4 | Scope detection picks wrong base branch | **High** | Small if Option A; medium if Option C |

Want me to:

1. **File the four issues as GitHub issues** with the diagnostic context above so they're tracked?
2. **Dig into the codex-wrong-scope one** (#4) to confirm exactly which branch was picked and why — since "this was just merged" suggests there might have been a recent regression worth tracing?
3. **Both** — file all four, then take #4 as the immediate next investigation since it's user-visible and behavioral?

Or just leave them in this conversation as a record? Your call.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The four bugs you're reporting share a common shape: each one *silently degrades* a feature that's documented to work better than it does. Failures don't crash, tokens don't error, drill-in doesn't say "no scroll available," and scope detection silently picks wrong. The review feature has a systemic observability gap, not four unrelated bugs. That suggests the right framing for the issues is "review observability sweep" with four sub-tickets, rather than four independent bugs — there's value in addressing them as a coordinated pass with a shared design principle ("review failures should always be diagnosable from the user's terminal output").
- Bug #4 (scope detection) is the kind of design choice where the original author was solving a real problem (stacked PRs) and the heuristic was correct for that case, but the heuristic's domain was much narrower than the real-world cases it now handles. The "most-recent tip wins" rule works perfectly when stacked PRs are the only non-main ancestor branches; it fails immediately when stale local branches exist, which describes most real developer machines. This is a pattern worth naming: heuristics tuned to the implementer's mental model break for users whose mental model differs. A `--base` flag (Option B) is often the right answer not because heuristics are bad, but because *users disagree about what the correct heuristic is* and the codebase shouldn't have to pick one.
- The fact that you said "I thought we fixed this" about #4 is itself a useful diagnostic — it suggests there was a prior PR that improved scope detection partially without fixing the underlying design. Worth a `git log -p cmd/entire/cli/review/scope.go` to find what was changed and what was left undone. The list of "Add prompt composition and scope detection" commits suggests the area has had multiple passes; the bug surviving them all is evidence the fundamental approach (timestamp heuristic) needs reconsidering, not just patching.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`
we should definetly tackle all four, but which ones do you tihnk should be first? the codex one?

Honestly, no — I'd argue **#1 (agent failure diagnostics)** first, then #4. Here's my reasoning, then push back if you disagree.

**Why #1 first**

It's a force-multiplier on every other fix. Right now if you change scope detection (#4), kick off a real review to verify, and the run fails — you have no idea whether your fix broke something or it was an unrelated agent crash. With #1 in place, you'd see exactly why, and your verification cycle for every subsequent bug shrinks from "guess and re-run" to "read the error and decide."

It's also the cheapest of the four:
- Likely 1–2 files (`run.go`/`run_multi.go` + sink rendering)
- No design debate (the fix is just "render `RunError.Err` to the user")
- Mirrors this current PR's principle: observability before behavior

And it has the same shape as the PR we just shipped — silent failure → user-visible message. The pattern is fresh in your head.

**Why #4 second, not first**

#4 is the highest *user impact* (wastes tokens on every wrong-scope run, which is real money), but the actual fix isn't "change a line of code" — it's a design question requiring a brainstorm:

- Option A: invert priority (mainline-first, heuristic-fallback)
- Option B: add `--base <ref>` flag
- Option C: probe `gh pr view` for PR target
- Option D: require picked base to be ancestor of mainline

You'd want to think through which of these fits your workflow before writing code. That's a 30-min discussion with whoever owns review (you?). Meanwhile #1 can be shipping in the background.

**Other reason to do #1 first: it derisks #4's verification.**

The way to validate #4's fix is to run real reviews on branches with various ancestor topologies and confirm the right base is picked. Some of those reviews will probably fail for unrelated reasons (network, agent CLI hiccups, env handshake). Without #1, every such failure is a black box and you're back to manual log-spelunking. With #1, failures are self-explaining.

**Suggested order**

1. **#1** — agent failure diagnostics. Small, no design debate, ships fast.
2. **#4** — scope detection. Needs design call first; pick an option, then implement.
3. **#3** — drill-in scrolling. Medium UX work, no urgency given DumpSink workaround.
4. **#2** — tokens column. Either trivial (parser missing emit) or out of scope (agent CLI doesn't surface tokens). Investigate-then-decide.

**Where you might disagree**

If you'd rather pick by "what bugs me most when using review," not "what's most efficient to ship," then #4 absolutely first — it's the one that wastes your time per-invocation and frustrates you. The token waste of even one wrong-scope review run probably exceeds the engineering cost of #1, so the ROI math actually favors #4 if you're optimizing for *near-term cost saved* rather than *long-term debugging speed*.

Honest answer: both orderings are defensible. I lean #1 first because of the compounding leverage; you might lean #4 first because the user-facing pain is more visceral. Whichever you pick, the *parallel* path is to start the #4 design discussion now (in chat, async — Option A vs B vs C vs D) so when #1 ships, #4 has a clear path forward.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The "fix observability before behavior" principle isn't just a coding rule — it's a workflow accelerant. Every behavioral bug you fix afterward gets easier to verify because failures during verification are self-explaining instead of opaque. The dollar value of this compounds: if #1 reduces verification time on each subsequent bug by 50%, and you have three more bugs to fix, you've recouped #1's cost roughly 1.5× over before counting any direct user benefit. This is a pattern worth weighing whenever you have a "fix observability" PR competing against a "fix behavior" PR for sequencing.
- Bug #4 needs a design call before code, which is a real signal worth honoring. The temptation with high-impact bugs is "just fix it, we'll iterate on the design." But scope-detection picks happen *inside* every review run and shape the entire output — getting the design wrong burns a full agent run's worth of tokens to learn it was wrong. That's a different cost profile than a UI bug where iteration is cheap. Bugs whose verification cycle is expensive deserve more upfront design than bugs whose verification is cheap.
- The argument I gave for #1 first is a particular case of a more general heuristic: when ordering work, prefer items whose completion *changes the cost structure* of subsequent items. #1 changes the cost of debugging #2, #3, #4 (cheaper), so it has compounding value. #4 changes nothing about #1, #2, #3's cost. Heuristics like "do the highest-impact thing first" miss this — impact at the moment of completion isn't the same as impact through the rest of the work queue. Worth keeping in mind on bigger sprints where four-item ordering decisions become forty-item ordering decisions.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

35	// RunFinished writes a narrative block per agent, then a counts line.
36	func (s DumpSink) RunFinished(summary reviewtypes.RunSummary) {
37		for _, run := range summary.AgentRuns {
38			s.dumpAgent(run)
39		}
40		s.dumpCounts(summary)
41	}

43	// dumpAgent composes one agent's section as markdown and writes it through
44	// mdrender. The counts line at the end of the run is intentionally NOT
45	// rendered through markdown — it's a terse status summary that benefits
46	// from staying on a single uncolored line for grep-ability.
47	//
48	// Markdown structure per agent:
49	//
50	//	# <name> review
51	//	(optional status line for cancelled / failed)
52	//	(optional blockquote for RunError events on failure)
53	//	(narrative — agent's AssistantText events joined)
54	func (s DumpSink) dumpAgent(run reviewtypes.AgentRun) {
55		var b strings.Builder
56		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "# %s review\n\n", run.Name)
57	
58		switch run.Status {
59		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled:
60			b.WriteString("_cancelled_\n")
61		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed:
62			// Surface the wait error if any (process exit failure), then any
63			// agent-level RunError events the parser emitted (typically a torn
64			// stdout stream — caught at the orchestrator level by classifyStatus
65			// even when the process itself exited 0).
66			if run.Err != nil {
67				fmt.Fprintf(&b, "**Failed:** `%v`\n\n", run.Err)
68			} else {
69				b.WriteString("**Failed**\n\n")
70			}
71			for _, ev := range run.Buffer {
72				if re, ok := ev.(reviewtypes.RunError); ok && re.Err != nil {
73					fmt.Fprintf(&b, "> agent error: `%v`\n\n", re.Err)
74				}
75			}
76			// Render any narrative text the agent produced before the failure
77			// surfaced — useful when the parser tore mid-response so reviewers
78			// can see partial output instead of a bare "(failed)" line.
79			if narrative := joinAssistantText(run.Buffer); narrative != "" {
80				b.WriteString(narrative)
81				b.WriteString("\n")
82			}
83		case reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded, reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown:
84			if narrative := joinAssistantText(run.Buffer); narrative != "" {
85				b.WriteString(narrative)
86				b.WriteString("\n")
87			}
88		}
89	
90		// RenderForWriter is TTY-aware: returns raw markdown for non-TTY writers,
91		// glamour-styled output otherwise. Errors are best-effort — fall back to
92		// raw markdown so the user always gets the content.
93		rendered, err := mdrender.RenderForWriter(s.W, b.String())
94		if err != nil {
95			rendered = b.String()
96		}
97		fmt.Fprint(s.W, rendered)
98	}

101	// them with newlines, trimming the result to keep dump output tight.
102	func joinAssistantText(buf []reviewtypes.Event) string {
103		var b strings.Builder
104		for _, ev := range buf {
105			if at, ok := ev.(reviewtypes.AssistantText); ok {
106				b.WriteString(at.Text)
107				b.WriteString("\n")
108			}
109		}
110		return strings.TrimSpace(b.String())
111	}

114		succ, fail, canc := 0, 0, 0
115		for _, r := range summary.AgentRuns {
116			switch r.Status {
117			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded:
118				succ++
119			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed:
120				fail++
121			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled:
122				canc++
123			case reviewtypes.AgentStatusUnknown:
124				// Unknown status: not counted in any bucket.
125			}
126		}
127		fmt.Fprintf(s.W, "%d agent(s) done — %d succeeded, %d failed, %d cancelled\n",
128			len(summary.AgentRuns), succ, fail, canc)

3	// run.go implements the single-agent orchestrator. CU8 generalizes
4	// to N agents with a sibling RunMulti that re-uses the same
5	// AgentRun classification and Sink fan-out.
6	package review
7	
8	import (
9		"context"
10		"fmt"
11		"time"
12	
13		reviewtypes "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/review/types"
14	)
15	
16	// Run executes a single-agent review. Events from the agent are forwarded
17	// to all sinks via AgentEvent as they arrive; on completion, RunFinished
18	// is called on each sink with the populated RunSummary.
19	//
20	// Returns the summary plus the agent's terminal error (nil on clean exit,
21	// ctx.Err() on cancellation, an error wrapping *exec.ExitError on non-zero
22	// exit, or an agent-level error when the event stream reports failure).
23	// Callers can inspect both: the summary is always populated even on error.
24	func Run(
25		ctx context.Context,
26		reviewer reviewtypes.AgentReviewer,
27		cfg reviewtypes.RunConfig,
28		sinks []reviewtypes.Sink,
29	) (reviewtypes.RunSummary, error) {
30		started := time.Now()
31	
32		proc, err := reviewer.Start(ctx, cfg)
33		if err != nil {
34			// Construction failed — classify (cancellation vs failure), fan out, return.
35			// No event-stream signals available since Start failed before producing any.
36			finished := time.Now()
37			status := classifyStatus(ctx, err, eventOutcome{})
38			summary := reviewtypes.RunSummary{
39				StartedAt:  started,
40				FinishedAt: finished,
41				Cancelled:  status == reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled,
42				AgentRuns: []reviewtypes.AgentRun{{
43					Name:      reviewer.Name(),
44					Status:    status,
45					Err:       err,
46					StartedAt: started,
47					Duration:  finished.Sub(started),
48				}},
49			}
50			for _, sink := range sinks {
51				sink.RunFinished(summary)
52			}
53			return summary, err //nolint:wrapcheck // interface-boundary passthrough; wrapping breaks classifyStatus's ctx.Err() identity check for cancelled-during-Start scenarios
54		}
55	
56		var (
57			buffer       []reviewtypes.Event
58			tokens       reviewtypes.Tokens
59			finishedSeen bool // saw Finished{...} event from the parser
60			finishedOk   bool // its Success field
61			sawRunError  bool // saw at least one RunError event
62			firstRunErr  error
63		)
64		for ev := range proc.Events() {
65			buffer = append(buffer, ev)
66			switch e := ev.(type) {
67			case reviewtypes.Tokens:
68				tokens = e // Tokens is cumulative per CU2 contract — overwrite.
69			case reviewtypes.Finished:
70				finishedSeen = true
71				finishedOk = e.Success
72			case reviewtypes.RunError:
73				sawRunError = true
74				if firstRunErr == nil {
75					firstRunErr = e.Err
76				}
77			}
78			for _, sink := range sinks {
79				sink.AgentEvent(reviewer.Name(), ev)
80			}
81		}
82	
83		waitErr := proc.Wait()
84		finished := time.Now()
85		status := classifyStatus(ctx, waitErr, eventOutcome{finishedSeen: finishedSeen, finishedOk: finishedOk, sawRunError: sawRunError})
86		runErr := waitErr
87		if runErr == nil && status == reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed {
88			runErr = agentRunFailureError(reviewer.Name(), firstRunErr)
89		}
90	
91		summary := reviewtypes.RunSummary{
92			StartedAt:  started,
93			FinishedAt: finished,
94			Cancelled:  status == reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled,
95			AgentRuns: []reviewtypes.AgentRun{{
96				Name:      reviewer.Name(),
97				Status:    status,
98				Tokens:    tokens,
99				Buffer:    buffer,
100				StartedAt: started,
101				Duration:  finished.Sub(started),
102				Err:       runErr,
103			}},
104		}
105		for _, sink := range sinks {
106			sink.RunFinished(summary)
107		}
108		return summary, runErr
109	}
110	
111	func agentRunFailureError(agent string, cause error) error {
112		if cause != nil {
113			return fmt.Errorf("review agent %s reported failure: %w", agent, cause)
114		}
115		return fmt.Errorf("review agent %s reported failure", agent)
116	}
117	
118	// eventOutcome summarises agent-level signals observed in the event stream.
119	// Used by classifyStatus to downgrade a process-level "exit 0" run that the
120	// parser flagged as torn (RunError + Finished{Success: false}) — a clean
121	// process exit doesn't imply a clean review result.
122	type eventOutcome struct {
123		finishedSeen bool // a Finished event was emitted (parser ran to completion)
124		finishedOk   bool // Finished.Success
125		sawRunError  bool // at least one RunError event was emitted
126	}
127	
128	// classifyStatus maps a process Wait error AND the event-stream outcome to
129	// a terminal AgentStatus.
130	//
131	// Order matters: ctx-cancelled + signal-killed delivers an *exec.ExitError
132	// with exit code -1, which would otherwise be misclassified as Failed.
133	// Check ctx.Err() FIRST so cancelled runs are reported as Cancelled.
134	// (Reference: PR #1018 commit 8e82e407a.)
135	//
136	// Event-level signals override process-level success: if the parser saw a
137	// RunError or emitted Finished{Success: false}, the run is Failed even when
138	// the process exits 0. This catches torn stdout streams the parser surfaces
139	// via RunError + Finished{Success: false} (CU3 fix-loop guarantee).
140	func classifyStatus(ctx context.Context, waitErr error, outcome eventOutcome) reviewtypes.AgentStatus {
141		if ctx.Err() != nil {
142			return reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled
143		}
144		if waitErr != nil {
145			return reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed
146		}
147		// Process exited cleanly (exit 0). Honor agent-level signals.
148		if outcome.sawRunError {
149			return reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed
150		}
151		if outcome.finishedSeen && !outcome.finishedOk {
152			return reviewtypes.AgentStatusFailed
153		}
154		return reviewtypes.AgentStatusSucceeded
155	}
