69		agentIdx int
70		ev       reviewtypes.Event
71	}
72	
73	// RunMulti executes a multi-agent review. Each reviewer runs concurrently;
74	// events from N agents are funneled into a single dispatch loop that calls
75	// every sink's AgentEvent in arrival order from a single goroutine
76	// (serial-dispatch guarantee).
77	//
78	// Returns the aggregated RunSummary plus the FIRST non-cancellation
79	// per-agent error encountered. Callers that want individual errors should
80	// inspect summary.AgentRuns[i].Err. The returned summary is always
81	// populated, even on error; sinks are always notified via RunFinished.
82	//
83	// Cancellation propagates through ctx; each reviewer's Process honors it.
84	// When ctx is cancelled all per-agent goroutines will eventually drain and
85	// the channel will close; RunMulti waits for all before calling RunFinished.
86	func RunMulti(
87		ctx context.Context,
88		reviewers []reviewtypes.AgentReviewer,
89		cfg reviewtypes.RunConfig,
90		sinks []reviewtypes.Sink,
91	) (reviewtypes.RunSummary, error) {
92		started := time.Now()
93	
94		if len(reviewers) == 0 {
95			summary := reviewtypes.RunSummary{
96				StartedAt:  started,
97				FinishedAt: started,
98				Cancelled:  ctx.Err() != nil,
99			}
100			for _, sink := range sinks {
101				sink.RunFinished(summary)
102			}
103			return summary, nil
104		}
105	
106		states := make([]*perAgentState, len(reviewers))
107		for i, r := range reviewers {
108			states[i] = &perAgentState{
109				name:      r.Name(),
110				startedAt: time.Now(),
111			}
112		}
113	
114		// fanIn carries tagged events from N agent goroutines into the single
115		// dispatch loop. Buffer of len(reviewers)*16 amortises goroutine
116		// scheduling jitter without holding an unbounded queue.
117		fanIn := make(chan taggedEvent, len(reviewers)*16)
118	
119		var wg sync.WaitGroup
120		for i, r := range reviewers {
121			proc, err := r.Start(ctx, cfg)
122			if err != nil {
123				states[i].startErr = err
124				states[i].finishedAt = time.Now()
125				continue
126			}
127			states[i].proc = proc
128			wg.Add(1)
129			go func(idx int, p reviewtypes.Process) {
130				defer wg.Done()
131				for ev := range p.Events() {
132					fanIn <- taggedEvent{agentIdx: idx, ev: ev}
133				}
134				states[idx].waitErr = p.Wait()
135				states[idx].finishedAt = time.Now()
136			}(i, proc)
137		}
138	
139		// Close fanIn after all forwarding goroutines finish. This goroutine
140		// must be launched AFTER all wg.Add calls above so the WaitGroup
141		// counter is correct before Wait is called.
142		go func() {
143			wg.Wait()
144			close(fanIn)
145		}()
146	
147		// Dispatch loop: runs on the caller's goroutine (no extra goroutine).
148		// Ranges over fanIn until it is closed, updating per-agent state and
149		// forwarding to sinks serially — the serial-dispatch contract holds
150		// even though N agent goroutines emit concurrently.
151		for tagged := range fanIn {
152			st := states[tagged.agentIdx]
153			st.buffer = append(st.buffer, tagged.ev)
154			switch e := tagged.ev.(type) {
155			case reviewtypes.Tokens:
156				st.tokens = e // Tokens is cumulative — overwrite, don't sum.
157			case reviewtypes.Finished:
158				st.finishedSeen = true
159				st.finishedOk = e.Success
160			case reviewtypes.RunError:
161				st.sawRunError = true
162			default:
163				// Started, AssistantText, ToolCall — no state to update.
164			}
165			for _, sink := range sinks {
166				sink.AgentEvent(st.name, tagged.ev)
167			}
168		}
169	
170		// All goroutines have exited; all waitErr fields are set.
171		finished := time.Now()
172		cancelled := ctx.Err() != nil
173	
174		agentRuns := make([]reviewtypes.AgentRun, len(states))
175		var firstErr error
176		for i, st := range states {
177			var status reviewtypes.AgentStatus
178			if st.startErr != nil {
179				status = classifyStatus(ctx, st.startErr, eventOutcome{})
180			} else {
181				status = classifyStatus(ctx, st.waitErr, eventOutcome{
182					finishedSeen: st.finishedSeen,
183					finishedOk:   st.finishedOk,
184					sawRunError:  st.sawRunError,
185				})
186			}
187			agentErr := st.startErr
188			if agentErr == nil {
189				agentErr = st.waitErr
190			}
191			agentRuns[i] = reviewtypes.AgentRun{
192				Name:      st.name,
193				Status:    status,
194				Tokens:    st.tokens,
195				Buffer:    st.buffer,
196				StartedAt: st.startedAt,
197				Duration:  st.finishedAt.Sub(st.startedAt),
198				Err:       agentErr,
199			}
200			if firstErr == nil && agentErr != nil && status != reviewtypes.AgentStatusCancelled {
201				firstErr = agentErr
202			}
203		}
204	
205		summary := reviewtypes.RunSummary{
206			StartedAt:  started,
207			FinishedAt: finished,
208			Cancelled:  cancelled,
209			AgentRuns:  agentRuns,
210		}
211		for _, sink := range sinks {
212			sink.RunFinished(summary)
213		}
214	
215		return summary, firstErr
216	}

4	// alt-screen drill-in view. It renders one agent's live event buffer with
5	// header/footer chrome and pads to exactly termHeight lines so every frame
6	// has the same line count (avoids ghost rows in the Bubble Tea alt-screen
7	// frame diff).
8	package review

15	)

17	// eventLine converts a single Event to a single display line for the detail
18	// view. The line is stripped of control sequences and truncated to maxWidth
19	// display cells.
20	func eventLine(ev reviewtypes.Event, maxWidth int) string {
21		var raw string
22		switch e := ev.(type) {
23		case reviewtypes.Started:
24			raw = "[started]"
25		case reviewtypes.AssistantText:
26			raw = e.Text
27		case reviewtypes.ToolCall:
28			raw = fmt.Sprintf("[tool: %s] %s", e.Name, e.Args)
29		case reviewtypes.Tokens:
30			raw = fmt.Sprintf("[tokens in=%d out=%d]", e.In, e.Out)
31		case reviewtypes.Finished:
32			if e.Success {
33				raw = "[finished: success]"
34			} else {
35				raw = "[finished: failed]"
36			}
37		case reviewtypes.RunError:
38			if e.Err != nil {
39				raw = fmt.Sprintf("[error: %v]", e.Err)
40			} else {
41				raw = "[error]"
42			}
43		default:
44			raw = "[unknown event]"
45		}
46	
47		return truncateDisplayWidth(sanitizeDisplayText(raw), maxWidth)
48	}
49	
50	// detailView renders the alt-screen drill-in for one agent. row is the agentRow
51	// being inspected. termWidth/termHeight come from WindowSizeMsg.
52	//
53	// Rendering:
54	//  1. Header line: "─── <name> (<n> events) ─────────────" (filled to termWidth)
55	//  2. Body: events from row.buffer scrolled to detailScroll, one line each,
56	//     sanitized and truncated to termWidth display cells.
57	//  3. Footer line: "←/→ switch agent · Esc back · ↑/↓ scroll"
58	//
59	// CRITICAL: the rendered string is padded to exactly termHeight lines so every
60	// frame has the same line count. Bubble Tea's alt-screen frame diff leaves ghost
61	// rows if the line count varies between frames.
62	func detailView(row agentRow, detailScroll, termWidth, termHeight int) string {
63		if termWidth < 1 {
64			termWidth = 80
65		}
66		if termHeight < 3 {
67			termHeight = 3
68		}
69	
70		// Reserve 1 line for header, 1 for footer; the body fills the rest.
71		bodyHeight := termHeight - 2
72		if bodyHeight < 0 {
73			bodyHeight = 0
74		}
75	
76		// 1. Header line.
77		headerContent := fmt.Sprintf("─── %s (%d events) ", sanitizeDisplayText(row.name), len(row.buffer))
78		header := padDisplayWidthWith(headerContent, termWidth, "─")
79	
80		// 2. Body lines.
81		lines := buildBodyLines(row.buffer, detailScroll, bodyHeight, termWidth)
82	
83		// Pad body to exactly bodyHeight lines.
84		for len(lines) < bodyHeight {
85			lines = append(lines, strings.Repeat(" ", termWidth))
86		}
87	
88		// 3. Footer line.
89		footerText := "←/→ switch agent · Esc back · ↑/↓ scroll"
90		footer := padDisplayWidth(footerText, termWidth)
91	
92		// Assemble: header + body + footer = termHeight lines total.
93		var b strings.Builder
94		b.WriteString(header)
95		b.WriteString("\n")
96		for _, line := range lines {
97			b.WriteString(line)
98			b.WriteString("\n")
99		}
100		b.WriteString(footer)
101		// No trailing newline after footer — the caller (View) adds its own.
102	
103		return b.String()
104	}
105	
106	// buildBodyLines computes the visible body lines for the detail view.
107	// It takes the full event buffer, a scroll offset, the maximum number of lines
108	// to show, and the column width. Returns at most bodyHeight lines.
109	func buildBodyLines(buffer []reviewtypes.Event, scroll, bodyHeight, termWidth int) []string {
110		if len(buffer) == 0 || bodyHeight <= 0 {
111			return nil
112		}
113	
114		// Clamp scroll to valid range.
115		if scroll < 0 {
116			scroll = 0
117		}
118		if scroll >= len(buffer) {
119			scroll = len(buffer) - 1
120		}
121	
122		// Determine window: scroll is the index of the LAST visible line so the
123		// user sees the most-recent events when auto-scrolling. Work backwards.
124		end := scroll + 1 // exclusive upper bound
125		start := end - bodyHeight
126		if start < 0 {
127			start = 0
128		}
129		// Clamp end to buffer length.
130		if end > len(buffer) {
131			end = len(buffer)
132			start = end - bodyHeight
133			if start < 0 {
134				start = 0
135			}
136		}
137	
138		lines := make([]string, 0, end-start)
139		for i := start; i < end; i++ {
140			lines = append(lines, eventLine(buffer[i], termWidth))
141		}
142		return lines
143	}

Fish quirk — `$PATH` is a list, so `env PATH=/tmp/fake-bin:$PATH` does cartesian-product expansion (produces multiple `PATH=...` args, last one wins with a *single* original entry). Result: the actual `PATH` only contains `/tmp/fake-bin` plus one path component, so `git` isn't findable, hence the "Not a git repository" error from `paths.WorktreeRoot`.

Fix — join `$PATH` explicitly:

```fish
env PATH=/tmp/fake-bin:(string join : $PATH) /tmp/entire-failtest review
```

Or use bash for the invocation (handles `:$PATH` natively):

```fish
bash -c 'PATH=/tmp/fake-bin:$PATH /tmp/entire-failtest review'
```

Either should work. The `(string join : $PATH)` version is more fish-native; the `bash -c` version is identical to the bash recipe I originally gave you. Pick whichever reads cleaner.

That's exactly bug #4 you flagged earlier — scope detection picking the wrong branch. It's hitting because:

- `origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool` exists as a remote-tracking ref in your local repo
- Its tip commit is an ancestor of your HEAD (because it got merged into main, which you just merged into your branch)
- `detectScopeBaseRef` picks the merged ancestor with the **most recent committerdate** — and that branch was the most recently advanced before its merge

Your local probably still has stale refs for branches that were deleted on the remote after merge. Cleaning them up gives you the right scope back, at least until the next time this happens:

```fish
git remote prune origin
```

- The git fetch behavior is the structural amplifier here: by default `git fetch origin` updates *every* `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` regardless of whether the branch is "alive" in workflow terms. The more active your team is on feature branches, the more likely the picker chooses one of those over mainline. So the bug gets WORSE as the codebase gets more active — which is exactly when reviewing against the right base matters most. Heuristics that punish their own success conditions are a strong signal that the underlying axis is wrong, not just miscalibrated.

Three real issues in your report — let me triage:

**1. The script is broken — my recipe's fault.**

That bash error in your stderr (`Authentication failed. Run claude login.: command not found`) is the fake binary itself failing to parse. Either fish's `printf` quoting got mangled in your shell, or copy-paste broke something. Switch to a more robust recipe that doesn't depend on escape interpretation:

```fish
mkdir -p /tmp/fake-bin
echo '#!/bin/bash' > /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'echo "Error: invalid_api_key" >&2' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'echo "Authentication failed. Run claude login." >&2' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'echo "Hint: see docs.claude.com/cli/auth" >&2' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'exit 1' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
chmod +x /tmp/fake-bin/claude
```

Verify: `/tmp/fake-bin/claude; echo "exit: $status"` — should show three clean stderr lines, no bash errors, `exit: 1`.

**2. "✓ done" instead of "✗ failed" in the dashboard — bigger bug than my PR currently fixes.**

You spotted something my fix doesn't address. Look at this from your output:

```
claude-code           ✓ done      2ms
1 agent(s) done — 0 succeeded, 1 failed, 0 cancelled
```

The row says `✓ done`, the tally says `1 failed`. Inconsistent. Here's why:

When `claude` (your fake) exits, the parser reads stdout to EOF and emits `Finished{Success: true}` because it saw a clean stream close — the parser doesn't know about the exit code. The TUI marks the row Succeeded based on that event. The orchestrator then calls `proc.Wait()`, gets the non-zero exit + stderr (a `*ProcessError`), and classifies the run as Failed in the final summary. The TUI's `runFinishedMsg` handler explicitly *preserves* the parser's Succeeded marking and only updates Unknown rows — so the row stays ✓ done forever.

For multi-agent this is much worse than your fast smoke test made visible: claude fails in 2ms, codex runs for 7 minutes, the dashboard shows claude as `✓ done` for the whole 7 minutes. Exactly the "shouldn't give them nothing" complaint.

The real fix needs the orchestrator to emit a synthetic `RunError{waitErr}` event into the sink stream right after `proc.Wait()` returns a non-nil error. The TUI already handles `RunError` correctly (sets row.status=Failed, row.err=waitErr), so the live preview I added would then fire. This needs ~10 lines added to `run.go` and `run_multi.go`, plus a small dedup in `dump.go` so the same error doesn't render twice.

**3. Dump rendering "looks bad" — partly from the broken script, partly real.**

Your output shows weirdness like `Hint: see\n  docs.claude.com/cli/auth` wrapping mid-URL. Some of that is glamour's terminal-width wrapping inside the code fence — unavoidable on narrow terminals, but tolerable. The bigger ugliness in your output is the bash syntax error inside the stderr block (`line 4: Authentication failed...: command not found`), which is from the broken fake binary, not the rendering. With a working fake, the fenced block reads clean.

**4. "Is the only error you checked for api error?"**

No, the fix is generic. The `*ProcessError` type captures any process exit failure with stderr, regardless of *what* the agent's stderr says (auth errors, network timeouts, license issues, segfaults that emit stack traces, etc.). All of them get the fenced-block rendering. Anything *not* a `*ProcessError` (e.g., a generic `errors.New(...)` from somewhere upstream) keeps the inline rendering — backward compatible with the four existing failure-rendering tests.

**Next step**

The "✓ done despite failure" bug (#2 above) is what's actually biting you in the multi-agent scenario. My current PR doesn't fix it. I'd recommend extending this PR to also emit synthetic `RunError` from the post-`Wait()` path so the TUI flips to ✗ failed live, mid-run. ~30-40 lines including a test, same TDD discipline.

To your question: **no, it captures any non-zero process exit, not just auth.** The auth message in your fake binary was illustrative; the actual mechanism is generic.

The fix triggers whenever `proc.Wait()` returns a non-nil error, which happens for *any* non-zero exit code. That includes the realistic agent failure modes:

| Failure mode | Exit behavior | Captured? |
|---|---|---|
| Auth / API key invalid | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| Network timeout | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| Rate limit hit | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| Quota / license exceeded | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| Wrong model name | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| File permission errors | non-zero + stderr | ✓ |
| Segfault / crash | non-zero (signal exit) + partial stderr | ✓ |
| OOM killed | non-zero (137) + maybe no stderr | ✓ (header without fenced block) |
| Torn stdout mid-response | parser RunError (already existed) | ✓ |
| Scanner error mid-read | parser RunError (already existed) | ✓ |
| Process exits 0 silently | nothing | ✗ |
| Process hangs forever | nothing until you Ctrl+C | ✗ (cancellation path) |

Whatever the agent CLI prints to stderr before exiting non-zero ends up in the live preview and the post-run fenced block. So a network timeout reads `error: codex: exit status 1: stderr: Connection timed out…` in the preview live, with full multi-line stderr (DNS hint, retry suggestion, etc.) in the dump.

**The two failure modes NOT captured** are both edge cases:
1. *Silent success* — agent exits 0 but produces no useful output. Looks like a clean run with empty narrative. Rare in practice; agents either output review findings or fail loudly.
2. *Hung process* — never exits, you Ctrl+C to cancel. That goes through the cancellation path (`AgentStatusCancelled`), separate UX from failure.

So in practice this should surface essentially all failures users actually hit. The auth-style stderr in your test is just one shape — the same code path renders any other stderr shape identically.

If you want extra confidence, swap the fake binary's stderr to simulate a different real-world error and re-run — the rendering will be identical:

```fish

echo 'echo "Error: rate limit exceeded (RPS quota)" >&2' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'echo "Retry after: 47s" >&2' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
echo 'exit 1' >> /tmp/fake-bin/claude
env PATH=/tmp/fake-bin:(string join : $PATH) /tmp/entire-failtest review --agent claude-code
```

Same flow, different message — and the preview should show `error: claude-code: exit status 1: stderr: Error: rate limit exceeded…` instead of the auth one. If that works, we have generic coverage.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The right framing for "does X cover all cases?" questions is to look at the *abstraction level* of the trigger condition, not the example. My trigger is "process exit non-zero" which is an abstract category covering thousands of concrete failure shapes; the auth message was just one shape I picked for the smoke test fixture. This is the same reason `*ProcessError` itself is generic — it captures `*exec.ExitError + stderr` regardless of what caused the exit code, which is the level at which "everything that fails this way" can be uniformly handled.
- Worth noting that the *one* class of failures the fix can't reach — silent successes (exit 0 with empty narrative) — is also a failure mode users could legitimately confuse with success. If an agent gets booted off mid-thought by an auth refresh and exits cleanly, you'd see "✓ done" with no findings rendered. That's a separate problem from this PR but worth a future ticket: detect "exit 0 with zero AssistantText events" and surface a "review produced no output" warning.
- Also worth naming: the failure mode you'd want to ABSOLUTELY catch — agents lying about success — isn't in this category. Claude-code or codex returning a successful exit code with bogus content (hallucinated findings, wrong scope, etc.) is a content-quality issue not a process-failure issue. Process-level fixes can't help; you'd need response validation or cross-checking, which is much further afield.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

feat(review): surface agent failures in live dashboard and post-run dump

Three coordinated changes that make agent failures legible to the user
instead of silently displayed as "✓ done" or buried inside an inline-code
span:

1. run.go and run_multi.go: when proc.Wait() returns a non-nil error,
   emit a synthetic RunError event into the live sink stream. Previously
   the wait error only reached sinks via RunFinished — which fires once
   at the end of all agents. In a multi-agent run, an agent that exits
   non-zero in the first second would render as "✓ done" (from the
   parser's typical clean-EOF Finished{Success:true}) for the entire
   duration of any other still-running agent. The synthetic event flips
   the row to "✗ failed" within milliseconds of the failure, while
   other agents continue normally.

2. tui_model.go: when an agent has failed and row.err is set, render
   the error in the dashboard PREVIEW column instead of leaving it
   blank. The new formatErrorPreview helper strips wrapper noise:
   for *ProcessError it returns the first non-empty stderr line
   (the agent CLI's own headline message), since the agent name is
   already shown in column 1 and "✗ failed" in column 2 — no need
   to repeat them. For other error types it returns err.Error()
   verbatim, since they don't have wrappers worth stripping.

3. dump.go: when run.Err is a *ProcessError carrying captured stderr,
   render the failure block as a header line ("**Failed:** `agent`
   exited (`exit status N`). Stderr:") followed by the full stderr
   in a fenced code block on its own. Multi-line stderr (auth errors,
   stack traces, retry hints) reads cleanly instead of getting

## Summary

Three coordinated changes that make agent failures legible to the user instead of silently displayed as `✓ done` or buried inside an inline-code span:

1. **`run.go` / `run_multi.go`** — emit a synthetic `RunError` event into the live sink stream when `proc.Wait()` returns a non-nil error, so failures reach the TUI mid-run instead of only via the final `RunFinished` summary. Without this, in a multi-agent run a fast-failing agent shows `✓ done` for the entire duration of any other still-running agent (the parser's clean-EOF `Finished{Success:true}` doesn't reflect the actual exit code).
2. **`tui_model.go`** — when a row has failed and `row.err` is set, surface the error in the dashboard PREVIEW column instead of leaving it blank. New `formatErrorPreview` helper strips wrapper noise: for `*ProcessError` it returns the first non-empty stderr line directly (the agent CLI's headline message), since agent name and `✗ failed` status are already shown in adjacent columns. Generic errors render verbatim.
3. **`dump.go`** — when `run.Err` is a `*ProcessError` carrying captured stderr, render the failure block as `**Failed:** \`agent\` exited (\`exit status N\`). Stderr:` followed by the full stderr in a fenced code block. Multi-line agent output (auth errors, retry hints, stack traces) reads cleanly. Synthetic `RunError` events whose `Err` matches `run.Err` are skipped from the blockquote loop to avoid double-printing.

## Background

User-reported issue: when one agent in a multi-agent review fails, the dashboard shows `✗ failed` (or worse, `✓ done` due to the parser/exit-code mismatch) with an empty PREVIEW column for the entire remaining run duration. The post-run dump did show the failure, but only after dismissing the TUI — meaning during a 7-minute codex run, the user couldn't tell why claude had failed 2 minutes in. The dump rendering also crammed multi-line stderr into a single inline-code span, making it visually unreadable even after dismissal.

This change makes failures legible at three different points:
- **Live dashboard**: PREVIEW column shows the first stderr line (truncated with `…` per terminal width)
- **Ctrl+O drill-in**: same `RunError` event surfaces in the event buffer (truncation limitation noted below — separate ticket)
- **Post-run dump**: full stderr in a fenced code block, no truncation

## Coverage

The trigger is `proc.Wait()` returning non-nil — covers any non-zero process exit:

| Failure mode | Captured? |
|---|---|
| Auth / API key invalid | ✓ |
| Network timeout | ✓ |
| Rate limit hit | ✓ |
| Quota / license exceeded | ✓ |
| Wrong model name | ✓ |
| File permission errors | ✓ |
| Segfault / signal kill | ✓ |
| OOM kill (no stderr) | ✓ (header without fenced block) |
| Torn stdout mid-response | ✓ (existing parser-emitted RunError, unchanged) |
| Process exits 0 silently | ✗ (separate concern — empty-narrative detection) |
| Process hangs forever | ✗ (cancellation path) |

- Doesn't fix Ctrl+O drill-in truncation (`tui_detail.go:eventLine` still truncates each event to terminal width). The dashboard preview is more readable for the failure case but the detail view is unchanged. **Separate ticket** — needs proper viewport scrolling/wrapping.

  - Codex row continues running normally
  - Post-run dump shows fenced block with all stderr lines readable
  - Tested both auth-error and network-timeout shapes — same rendering, different message

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec review loop** — dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent with precisely crafted review context (never your session history); fix issues and re-dispatch until approved (max 5 iterations, then surface to human)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot

    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];

}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Review Loop:**
After writing the spec document:

1. Dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent (see spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md)
2. If Issues Found: fix, re-dispatch, repeat until Approved
3. If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:

A few specific design points to confirm before I write the spec:

1. **`--base` flag UX**: simple long flag `--base <ref>`, no short form (`-b` collides with cobra conventions). Accept any rev-parse-able ref (branch, tag, commit SHA). If the ref doesn't exist, fail loudly with `unknown ref: <X>` and exit non-zero before spawning agents — no silent fallback to default.

2. **Fallback chain order**: keep current order (`origin/main → origin/master → main → master`), drop `origin/HEAD` from the head of the chain since it's almost always a symbolic ref to `origin/main` — redundant. Or keep `origin/HEAD` for forks where it points elsewhere?

3. **Banner**: existing format `Reviewing <branch> vs <base>: N commits, M files changed, K uncommitted` works as-is — it already shows what was picked, so users can sanity-check. Optional: when `--base` was passed, prefix with `(--base override)` so the user knows their flag was respected.

4. **Empty repo / detached HEAD / no fallback ref exists**: error out with actionable message (`no mainline branch found; pass --base <ref> to specify`), don't crash.

That symptom is exactly explained by the same bug. Here's the chain:

The prompt that reaches codex is composed in `prompt.go:46`:
```
Scope: review only the commits unique to this branch vs origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool.
```

When the base is `origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool`, codex faithfully reviews `origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool...HEAD`. That range is computed by git as "commits in HEAD not in the base." Since `origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool` was merged into main *before* you branched, it's an ancestor of main but lots of mainline commits came after it. So `<base>...HEAD` includes:

- Every commit that landed on main *after* `soph/add-codex-post-tool` was merged (PRs #1145, #1150, #1157, #1158, #1163, #1166, etc.)
- *Plus* your actual branch commits

That's why the review "had nothing to do with your branch" — the scope was technically correct given the (wrong) base, but it dragged in 30+ commits of unrelated work, drowning your actual diff in noise. Codex wasn't ignoring the scope; it was reviewing exactly what we told it to, and what we told it to was wrong.

Approach A fixes both symptoms with one change. When base = `origin/main`, the scope range `origin/main...HEAD` is exactly the commits unique to your branch — codex reviews only your work, no upstream noise. No separate codex-specific fix needed.

You'll see this concretely after the fix lands: with `--base origin/main` (the new default), codex's review prose will start with something like *"I reviewed `origin/main...HEAD` — N commits"* instead of *"I reviewed `origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool...HEAD` — 31 commits"*. Same agent, correct base, vastly different content.

Good catch — that's a real issue, and it's actually a separate bug from #4. Let me clarify what's happening:

The prompt that goes to agents currently says (from `prompt.go:46`):
```
Scope: review only the commits unique to this branch vs origin/main.
```

The word "commits" is doing real work here — it explicitly tells the agent: only look at `origin/main..HEAD`, which includes only committed work. Uncommitted changes are excluded by design. Codex was being scrupulous about following that instruction.

That design choice makes sense if your mental model is "review what would be merged via PR." It does NOT match the more natural "review what I'm working on right now," especially when you're iterating fast and haven't committed yet.

**Two options:**

| Option | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **(a) Always include uncommitted** | Scope clause becomes "review the diff `<base>...HEAD` plus any uncommitted working-tree changes." Agent looks at both. Matches "review my work in progress" mental model. |
| **(b) Include uncommitted only when there's no committed work in scope** | If the branch is at base (0 commits unique), pivot to "review the uncommitted changes." Otherwise stay committed-only. Tries to detect intent. |

I'd recommend (a). Simpler, predictable, and matches what you just hit. Hidden gotcha with (b): when reviewing a feature branch where you've committed *some* work but are also iterating on uncommitted edits, those edits get silently skipped — same surprise factor as today.

This PR fixes bug #4 (scope detection picking wrong base) plus three related issues that surfaced during smoke testing. All changes live in `cmd/entire/cli/review/`.

**Four behavioral changes:**

1. **Default scope is mainline, not "closest merged ancestor"** — replaces the timestamp heuristic that was picking unrelated recently-merged feature branches (`origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool` etc.) as the review base. New default walks the fallback chain `origin/main → origin/master → main → master`. Deleted ~130 lines of heuristic code (`slowDetectScopeBaseRef`, `isAncestorOf`, candidate selection loop).

2. **`--base <ref>` flag for explicit override** — accepts any rev-parse-able ref (branch, tag, SHA). Validates with `git rev-parse --verify` before spawning agents so a typo errors immediately instead of after a 10-min review run. Stacked PR review (`--base feat/parent`) is now an explicit user action, not an inferred heuristic.

3. **Uncommitted changes are now in scope** — scope clause changed from `"review only the commits unique to this branch vs <ref>."` to `"review the commits unique to this branch vs <ref>, plus any uncommitted changes in the working tree."` Agents (codex confirmed in smoke test) now review your in-progress work, not just committed commits. Checkpoint context preserved as a separate prompt section.

4. **Three-dot diff in `countFilesChanged`** — was using `git diff base..HEAD` which over-counts files when mainline has advanced past the branch point (upstream-only changes appear as reversed deltas). Now uses `base...HEAD` (merge-base diff). Caught by codex during smoke; one-character fix in production code, no test could reliably reproduce it through testutil.

**Tests added/changed:**

- `TestDetectScopeBaseRef_PrefersMainOverAncestorBranches` — replaces `TestDetectScopeBaseRef_ClosestAncestorPreferred` (old test asserted opposite behavior)
- `TestComputeScopeStats_BaseOverrideUsed` / `_BaseOverrideUnknownRefErrors` / `_EmptyOverrideUsesMainlineDetection` — three new unit tests for the override path
- `TestComposeReviewPrompt_ScopeIncludesUncommittedChanges` — asserts the new scope clause wording
- `TestReviewCommandSmoke_BaseFlagThreadsThroughToPromptAndBanner` / `_BadBaseRefErrorsBeforeAgentSpawn` — two command-level tests that catch wiring bugs (would have caught the `silentErr` suppression bug I had to fix mid-smoke)
- Deleted `TestIsAncestorOf` (function deleted) and an attempted upstream-advance test that didn't actually reproduce the bug

**Smoke-verified end-to-end:**

- Banner shows `vs origin/main` not `vs origin/soph/add-codex-post-tool` ✓
- `--base no-such-ref` errors with exit code 1 and message naming the bad ref ✓
- Codex reviewed actual uncommitted scope.go/cmd.go/prompt.go changes (not just committed commits) ✓
- Codex's review itself found two real issues in this PR (three-dot fix + missing command-level test, both now addressed) ✓

**Net diff:** +43 lines (heuristic deletion outweighs flag wiring + tests), 6 files.

**What this PR does NOT do** (worth calling out in PR description):
- Doesn't change behavior for repos where mainline doesn't exist (fallback chain handles)
- Doesn't add a persistent default in settings — `--base` is per-invocation
- Doesn't touch `runGit` or other scope helpers
- Doesn't address the still-open Ctrl+O drill-in truncation (separate ticket)

Checkpoint context flow is intact end-to-end:

**Production plumbing (unchanged):**
- `runReview` (`cmd.go:382-383`) and `runMultiAgentPath` (`cmd.go:504-505`) still call `deps.ReviewCheckpointContext(ctx, worktreeRoot, scopeBaseRef)` to compute context from committed checkpoints in scope

- `ComposeReviewPrompt` (`prompt.go:54`) appends it as its own section in the prompt

**Prompt structure (the section ordering matters — checkpoint context comes AFTER scope clause):**

```
[skills]

[always-prompt]

[per-run-prompt]

Scope: review the commits unique to this branch vs <ref>, plus any uncommitted changes in the working tree. Ignore code outside this scope.

[checkpoint context — what the developer did, when, with what intent/outcome]
```

The new scope clause sits *between* the per-run prompt and the checkpoint context — the checkpoint section is fully preserved, unchanged.

**Tests that explicitly assert checkpoint context still in prompt:**
- `TestComposeReviewPrompt_IncludesCheckpointContext` (prompt_test.go:64) — unit-level, asserts both the new scope clause AND the checkpoint context text appear in the same prompt
- `TestReviewCommandSmoke_IncludesCheckpointContextInPrompt` (review_context_test.go:142) — end-to-end through the cobra command, captures the actual prompt sent to the agent, asserts both `"Scope:"` and checkpoint detail (`"Checkpoint context from commits in scope:"`, the checkpoint ID, the summary) appear

Both tests passed in the most recent run. The "intentional differentiator that makes this review better than others" is fully preserved.

**One caveat worth noting:** `ReviewCheckpointContext` is computed from *committed checkpoints in the scope range* — so it surfaces checkpoint metadata for commits between `<base>` and HEAD. If the scope has 0 commits (like your smoke test where everything was uncommitted), there are no checkpoints to reference and the section is empty. That's correct behavior — checkpoints attach to commits, not to working-tree state — and your uncommitted-in-scope work is still reviewed via the new clause wording. On a branch with real commits, both flows fire: agent reviews the diff AND has checkpoint context about what each commit was for.
wht about sessions? should we add this to cover uncommited checkpoints?

Great question — and yes, this is a real gap. Let me think about it honestly.

**What we have now:**
- `ReviewCheckpointContext` reads from the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch — *committed* checkpoints attached to commits in the scope range
- If you have 0 commits (uncommitted work only), there's nothing in that committed branch yet → agents get the diff but no checkpoint metadata about the agent sessions that produced it

**What's missing:**
Sessions in progress produce *temporary checkpoints* on shadow branches (`entire/<commit-hash>-<worktreeHash>`) before they're condensed into the committed v1 branch on `git commit`. These contain exactly the metadata you'd want in a review: prompts, summaries, file changes, sub-agent work, intent/outcome. That data is sitting right there and we're not reading it for uncommitted scope.

**Should we add it?**

Yes — it's the natural completion of the "review work-in-progress" change. Without it, the agent sees your uncommitted code diff but no context about *why* each piece was added. The checkpoint-context differentiator you mentioned (the thing that makes Entire's review better than others) only fires for committed work today.

**But it's a non-trivial follow-up, not a trivial add to this PR:**

| Design question | Options |
|---|---|
| Which sessions count? | All active sessions in this worktree? Just the most recent? All sessions on this branch's shadow branch? |
| How to format? | Same "Commits in scope" pattern but for temp checkpoints? Or a separate section ("In-progress sessions on this branch")? |
| Multi-session handling | Multi-agent runs and concurrent sessions can interleave on the same shadow branch — how to attribute checkpoints? |
| Pruning / redaction | Temporary checkpoints can contain unredacted prompts that haven't been processed yet — does the review-prompt path apply the same redaction the committed path does? |
| Filesize / token budget | A long agent session can produce dozens of checkpoints; how to cap without losing signal? |

**Recommendation:** ship this PR (#1175, scope detection + uncommitted-changes review) as-is since it's clean and tested, then open a focused follow-up PR for "include uncommitted session checkpoint context in review prompt." That follow-up deserves its own brainstorm because the design space above isn't obvious — and getting it wrong (e.g., dumping raw unredacted prompts into the agent prompt) has real downsides.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- That Bugbot finding is exactly the kind of "consistency at function boundaries" bug a human reviewer often misses on first pass. The function has *two* error paths (PlainOpen + ComputeScopeStats), each one had to independently honor the "fail-loud when baseOverride is set" contract, and only one of them did. The doc comment described the contract but the implementation matched it only partially. Static reasoning about whether all error paths preserve invariants is exactly what bots are good at — humans look at the happy path first and only notice the contract gap when the bug bites.
- The general pattern worth naming: any function whose documented contract has an exception condition (`if X then fail; otherwise degrade`) needs every early-exit point to evaluate X. If you only check at one of them, the contract is silently wrong at the others. Easy to grep for: search for `return "", nil` or similar "swallow the error" patterns in functions that have any error-naming contract in their doc, and audit each one.
- Worth noting that the failure mode this bug enabled (PlainOpen fails + `--base origin/main` given) is extremely rare in practice — you'd need a broken git directory, missing `.git`, or filesystem permission issues. So the bug is real but low-frequency. Still worth fixing because the cost of fixing (7 lines) is trivially below the cost of debugging the silent fallback if it ever does fire. Cheap consistency fixes are always worth taking.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec review loop** — dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent with precisely crafted review context (never your session history); fix issues and re-dispatch until approved (max 5 iterations, then surface to human)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Review Loop:**
After writing the spec document:

1. Dispatch spec-document-reviewer subagent (see spec-document-reviewer-prompt.md)
2. If Issues Found: fix, re-dispatch, repeat until Approved
3. If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:

Yes — bug #2 (tokens column always empty) is also fixed in this PR. The followup commits added a token-hydration pipeline:

**Data flow:**
1. Agent's lifecycle hooks (UserPromptSubmit, Stop) record token usage into the session state file — that's already part of the existing entire infrastructure, not new code
2. `RunConfig.EnrichAgentRun` hook is set to `reviewAgentRunTokenEnricher(worktreeRoot, headSHA)` (cmd.go:554) — looks up session state by agent name + start time + worktree, extracts tokens
3. **Multi-agent** (run_multi.go:141): after each agent's `Wait()`, the per-agent goroutine calls `emitEnrichedAgentTokens` which pushes a synthetic `Tokens` event into the fanIn channel. The TUI dispatch picks it up and updates `row.tokens` live as each agent finishes
4. **Single-agent** (run.go:117): `enrichRunSummary` hydrates `summary.AgentRuns[i].Tokens`, then `runFinishedMsg` in the TUI (tui_model.go:143-145) propagates that to `row.tokens` at RunFinished time — populated before the user dismisses the dashboard

**What users see now:**
- **Multi-agent dashboard**: tokens column populates as each agent finishes (claude finishes 12 min, codex finishes 7 min — each row updates independently when its goroutine completes Wait)
- **Single-agent dashboard**: tokens populate at "Press any key to exit" time

does option 1, take ones only related to the chanhes on teh branch?

Yes — with one nuance worth knowing about. Let me explain precisely.

**What option 1 actually filters by:**

A "session state file" has two fields that determine its shadow branch:
- `worktree_path` — which checkout the session ran in
- `base_commit` — what HEAD was when the session started

The shadow branch name is derived from both: `entire/<base_commit[:7]>-<worktreeHash[:6]>`. So "sessions on the current shadow branch" = sessions whose `worktree_path` matches your current worktree AND whose `base_commit` matches your current HEAD.

**Translated to your question — "only related to changes on the branch":**

| Session category | Included by option 1? |
|---|---|
| Active session you're running right now (current HEAD is its base) | ✅ Yes |
| Earlier session today, same base commit (you did claude work, then codex, both still uncommitted) | ✅ Yes |
| Session from before your last commit (its base_commit is older; its work has been condensed into committed checkpoints) | ❌ No — its checkpoint context is already on `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch and covered by the existing `ReviewCheckpointContext` for committed scope |
| Session from a different worktree or different branch | ❌ No |

So option 1 ≈ "sessions that contributed to changes on this branch SINCE your last commit" — i.e., the uncommitted work. The previously-committed work is already covered by the committed-checkpoint path that exists today. This makes the two paths *complementary*:

- Committed checkpoint context (today): "what each commit on this branch was for"
- Uncommitted session context (this design): "what the agents have been doing since the last commit"

Together, they cover the full picture of "what's been happening on this branch."

**The nuance:** if you started a session, did some work, committed it, then started a new session and did more work without committing, option 1 only catches the *current* session — not the earlier committed one. But that's correct, because the earlier session's work is already represented as a committed checkpoint and surfaced via the existing pathway.

Does that match your mental model of "only related to changes on the branch"? If yes, option 1 is the right answer. If you'd want session context for *previously committed* work too (e.g., to give the agent fuller history of how the branch evolved), that's a different design — but the existing committed-checkpoint pipeline already does that, and duplicating it for already-condensed sessions risks doubling the context.

content.text:
Now I'll present the design in sections. First section:

## Section 1: Scope & Where to Read From

**What it covers:** Active sessions whose state file in `.git/entire-sessions/` has `worktree_path` matching the current worktree AND `base_commit` matching the current HEAD. These are sessions currently contributing to uncommitted work on this branch. Read via the existing `session.StateStore.List(ctx)` API.

**What it explicitly excludes:** Sessions on previous base commits (their work is already committed; covered by existing committed-checkpoint context). Sessions from other worktrees. Sessions that have been fully condensed (`FullyCondensed: true`).

**Where the data flows:**

```
reviewCheckpointContext(ctx, worktreeRoot, scopeBaseRef)
  → existing committed-checkpoint logic (unchanged)
  → NEW: reviewSessionContext(ctx, worktreeRoot, headSHA) returns string
  → string concatenation: existingSection + "\n\n" + sessionSection
```

The new helper `reviewSessionContext` opens `session.NewStateStore`, lists states, filters by the criteria above, formats them, returns the section text. Lives in the same `review_context.go` file as the committed function — both produce sections of the same `CheckpointContext` prompt block, just from different sources.

Look right so far? If yes, I'll move to Section 2 (per-session formatting).
yes this is good

## Section 2: Per-Session Entry Format & Caps

**Each entry:** `  <session_id[:8]> <agent_name> "<first_prompt_truncated>" (touched: N files)`

Example block:
```
In-progress session context (uncommitted):
  019e0871 claude-code "Fix the scope detection bug — reviews are picking…" (touched: 3 files)
  019e0a23 codex "Add a regression test for the three-dot diff path…" (touched: 1 file)
```

**Data sources** (all already on session state):
- `session_id[:8]` — short identifier, enough to disambiguate visually
- `agent_name` — derived from `state.AgentType` (claude-code, codex, gemini-cli, etc.)
- `first_prompt` — the session's initial user prompt. Read from `prompt.txt` in the shadow-branch metadata for this session, truncated to 100 display chars with `…` if longer. Falls back to "(no prompt captured)" if unreadable.
- `files touched` — count from `state.FilesTouched` (already maintained by lifecycle hooks per turn). Renders nothing if 0, "(touched: N file/files)" otherwise.

**Caps to prevent prompt bloat:**
- **Max 5 sessions listed** — sorted newest-first by `state.StartedAt`. Append `  ...(N more sessions truncated)` if there are more.
- **Per-entry prompt truncation:** 100 display chars (matches the existing AssistantText truncation pattern in `tui_model.go:206`).
- **Total section budget:** soft cap ~1KB. If exceeded, drop entries from the bottom.

**Why first prompt and not latest:**
First prompt captures original intent ("fix bug X" / "add feature Y"). Latest prompt might be a refinement ("also handle edge case Z") that's confusing without context. Reviewer agents need to know what the *goal* was, not just what the last instruction said.

Look right? Two specific things worth your eye:

1. Is **5 sessions** the right cap? Most users have 1–2 active sessions, but if you regularly run more, raise this.
2. Is **"first prompt"** correct, or do you prefer **"latest prompt"** / **"all prompts concatenated and truncated"**?

Approve as-is or call out adjustments.
why are we capping? that loses context

You're right — capping at 5 was over-engineered. The token cost of even 50 sessions is trivial (~2KB), and you'd rather have full signal than lose it for theoretical bloat protection. The per-entry truncation (100 chars on prompt) is the same mistake — first prompts often contain real intent that gets clipped.

**Revised Section 2: No session count cap, full prompt per entry**

```
In-progress session context (uncommitted):
  019e0871 claude-code (touched: 3 files):
    Fix the scope detection bug — reviews are picking the wrong base
    branch because the timestamp heuristic prefers recently-merged
    feature branches over origin/main. Should default to mainline
    and add a --base flag for explicit override.
  019e0a23 codex (touched: 1 file):
    Add a regression test for the three-dot diff path so we don't
    regress to two-dot in the future.
```

**What changed:**
- **No session count cap.** Every matching session appears. If you have 20 active sessions, you see all 20 — that itself is diagnostic info.
- **Full first prompt per entry**, indented under the session header. No 100-char truncation. Multi-line OK — agents don't care about visual scanability, they parse text.
- **Session header on one line**, prompt body indented below. Makes the structure parseable for the agent without losing content.

**One sanity guard worth keeping** (the only "cap"):
A 50KB single prompt is pathological and indicates something wrong (a malformed prompt, an injection attempt, a paste accident). Keep a **per-prompt soft cap of 10KB** — if a single session's first prompt exceeds 10KB, truncate that entry's prompt with `… [N chars truncated, see session metadata]` and log at debug. This is rare and bounded.

Total prompt size: in normal use, 1–3 sessions × ~500 char prompts = ~2KB. In pathological use, capped at 10KB per session × 20 sessions = 200KB max — still inside any reasonable agent context window.

Does dropping the session cap and keeping only the 10KB-per-entry pathological guard match what you wanted? If yes, I'll move to Section 3 (error handling, redaction, edge cases).
how are we analyzing the checkpoints"? shouldnt we do something similar?

Great question — and the honest answer is the existing pipeline doesn't analyze at review time, it reads pre-generated summaries. Let me explain so you can decide if we should match that.

**How committed-checkpoint context works today:**

```
git commit
  → PostCommit hook
  → Strategy condenses session metadata to entire/checkpoints/v1
  → Summary provider (configured LLM) generates Intent + Outcome from session prompts + transcript
  → Intent/Outcome stored on the checkpoint as CommittedMetadata.Summary

Later: entire review
  → reviewCheckpointContext reads pre-generated Summary from v1 branch
  → renders "<commit_id> summary: <Intent>; <Outcome>"
```

So the LLM analysis happens at commit time (in the PostCommit hook), and review just *reads* the pre-baked summary. Cheap and fast at review time.

**For uncommitted sessions, the analog options:**

| Option | Cost | What reviewer sees |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Match the committed format — generate summary on-the-fly at review startup** | One LLM call per active session before review begins. Adds latency, can fail. | Synthesized Intent (no Outcome — session is in progress, outcome isn't known yet) |
| **B. Trigger early condensation (pre-emptive)** | Same LLM calls, but cached on the session state for subsequent reviews | Same as A, plus cached for next time |
| **C. Skip analysis, use raw prompts** (my proposal) | Free | First prompt verbatim — captures *user-stated* intent, not synthesized intent. Includes whatever noise was in the original prompt. |

**A subtle point:** the committed checkpoint's Summary has Intent + Outcome because the session *finished* before condensation. For in-progress sessions, "Outcome" is by definition not yet known. So even option A would only give us Intent — half the value of the committed pipeline's analysis.

**Tradeoff:**
- The reviewer agent gets *more* signal from a synthesized Intent than from a raw first prompt (cleaner, dedupes iteration noise)
- But it costs an LLM call at review startup AND the session might still be evolving (latest prompt could differ from initial)
- Worst case: synthesis lies because it's reading an incomplete narrative

**My recommendation:** start with option C (raw prompts) and revisit if the reviews aren't getting enough context. The cost of LLM-generating summaries per session at review startup is real, and the benefit over raw prompts is genuinely marginal when there's no outcome yet. We can layer summary generation in as a v2 once we see what actually helps.

But you have the final call here. Three answers:

1. **C** — raw prompts, ship soon, layer analysis later if needed
2. **A** — synthesize Intent on-the-fly at review startup, accept the LLM cost
3. **B** — pre-emptive condensation, fanciest but most invasive

Which?

content.text:
Exactly the right question to ask. Here's the existing fallback chain in `reviewCheckpointDetail` (review_context.go:107-135):

```
For each session in the checkpoint (newest first):
  1. Skip review-kind sessions
  2. If session has a Summary (Intent/Outcome/OpenItems):
       → format as "summary: <Intent>; <Outcome>; open: <first OpenItem>"
       → return immediately

If no session had a Summary:
  For each session again:
    3. Read prompts from the checkpoint metadata
    4. Use the LATEST prompt (loops backwards: prompts[len-1])
    5. Return "prompt: <truncated>"

If neither: return ""
```

Helpers already exist: `reviewSummaryText` (line 191) and `reviewPromptText` (line 203). Both run `stringutil.CollapseWhitespace` and `truncateReviewContextText`. Prefix is either `"summary: "` or `"prompt: "`.

**Implications for our design:**

1. **The committed pipeline already has a prompt-fallback path** — so option C (raw prompts) isn't a regression in consistency, it's the SAME pattern the existing code uses when summaries are missing. Our uncommitted-session entries will always go through the `"prompt: "` branch since summaries don't exist mid-session, but they'll match the format consistently.

2. **I had `first` prompt wrong.** The existing code uses **LATEST** (`prompts[len-1]`), not first. For consistency we should use latest too. Latest prompt typically captures current focus better than initial goal anyway.

3. **We can reuse `reviewPromptText` directly** — no new helper needed, just the same function applied to session-state-derived prompts instead of checkpoint-store prompts.

**Revised Section 2 entry format** (matching existing convention):

```
In-progress session context (uncommitted):
  019e0871 claude-code (touched: 3 files) prompt: <reviewPromptText output for latest prompt>
  019e0a23 codex (touched: 1 file) prompt: <reviewPromptText output for latest prompt>
```

`prompt:` prefix matches committed-pipeline output. `truncateReviewContextText` already applies sensible bounds (the helper's existing behavior, not a new cap). Falls back to nothing if no prompts captured.

This is cleaner than what I proposed earlier and stays consistent with the existing pattern. Pre-generated summaries for in-progress sessions remain a future optimization — when condensation runs eagerly enough, those sessions will naturally start populating `summary:` instead.

Sound right? Then I'll move to Section 3 (edge cases, error handling, where the helper lives, tests).
yes, so we're reusing what we already have

## Section 3: Implementation & Error Handling

**Where the helper lives:**

`reviewSessionContext(ctx, worktreeRoot, headSHA) string` in `cmd/entire/cli/review_context.go` — same file as the existing `reviewCheckpointContext`. Both produce sections from related data sources and need the same checkpoint/session package access, so co-locating keeps the cycle-free `cli` package boundary intact.

**Reading data — simpler than you'd expect:**

For active sessions, prompts are written to **the filesystem** at `<worktree>/.entire/metadata/<sessionID>/prompt.txt` during lifecycle hooks (`lifecycle.go:294-310`), separated by `\n\n---\n\n`. No need to open shadow branches — direct file reads. The committed pipeline reads from the shadow branch only because by then it's the only place; for in-progress sessions filesystem is canonical.

```
reviewSessionContext:
  store, _ := session.NewStateStore(ctx)
  states, _ := store.List(ctx)
  for state in states:
    if state.WorktreePath != worktreeRoot: skip
    if state.BaseCommit != headSHA: skip
    if state.FullyCondensed: skip
    if state.Kind == KindAgentReview: skip   // don't include the review session itself
    promptPath := <worktree>/.entire/metadata/<state.SessionID>/prompt.txt
    content, _ := os.ReadFile(promptPath)
    text := reviewPromptText(string(content))   // reuses existing helper
    append entry to section
  return formatted section or ""
```

**Edge cases:**

| Case | Behavior |
|---|---|
| No matching sessions | Return `""`. `ComposeReviewPrompt` already skips empty sections — no orphan section header. |
| Session has no prompt.txt yet (just spawned) | Skip that session in the section. Other sessions still included. |
| `StateStore.List` fails | Log at DEBUG, return `""`. The committed-context section still works; the run continues in degraded mode. Mirrors existing `reviewCheckpointContext` error handling. |
| `os.ReadFile` fails for one session | Skip that one, continue with others. Best-effort per session. |
| Filesystem prompt is stale vs. shadow-branch latest | The filesystem path is canonical-during-active-session (lifecycle.go writes it on every turn). If stale, the worst case is missing the most recent turn — acceptable for v1. |
| Concurrent session mid-write while we read | Read what's there. `os.ReadFile` gets the current snapshot; we don't lock. Stale reads are tolerable since the section is informational. |
| `state.Kind == KindAgentReview` | Skip — this is the agent that's *running the review*, not work to review. |

**Integration with prompt composition:**

Two minimal options for plumbing:

| | Option A: Extend `ReviewCheckpointContext` to also call `reviewSessionContext` | Option B: New `ReviewSessionContext` dep, two strings concatenated in `runReview` |
|---|---|---|
| Cycle risk | None — same package, same file | None |
| Test surface | One bridge function | Two |
| Future flexibility | Coupled — changes to either affect both | Independent |

**Recommend A.** The two sections always travel together in the prompt, so keeping their producer co-located avoids drifting interfaces. The function signature changes from `(ctx, worktreeRoot, scopeBaseRef)` to `(ctx, worktreeRoot, scopeBaseRef, headSHA)` — headSHA is already resolved upstream in `runReview` and passed to `RunConfig.StartingSHA`, so it's a free addition.

**Tests:**

- **Unit test in `review_context_test.go`**: `TestReviewSessionContext_IncludesActiveSession` — set up a temp repo, write a session state file with matching base/worktree, write a prompt.txt on disk, assert the returned section contains `prompt: <text>` for that session.
- **Unit test**: `TestReviewSessionContext_SkipsCondensedAndOtherWorktrees` — fixtures for excluded cases (FullyCondensed, mismatched worktree, mismatched base, KindAgentReview), assert each is skipped.
- **End-to-end**: extend `TestReviewCommandSmoke_IncludesCheckpointContextInPrompt` to also assert the "In-progress session context (uncommitted):" header appears when an active session state is present. Already has scaffolding for capturing the agent prompt.

Look right? If yes, the design is fully sketched — three sections (scope, format, implementation+errors). I'll skip writing the design doc to a file per your earlier instruction. Ready to either:

2. Build on top of `feat/review-base-flag-mainline-default` now (knowing it'll merge after #1175 to keep history linear)

feat(review): include in-progress session context in agent prompt

Extends the existing checkpoint-context pipeline to surface
uncommitted agent work alongside committed checkpoint summaries.
Without this, reviews of branches with only uncommitted work
(common case: developer mid-feature) lose the rich context that
makes Entire's review better than vanilla agent reviews — agents
see the diff but no signal about what each session was for.

reviewCheckpointContext is now a thin composer over two sources:

  reviewCheckpointContext(ctx, worktreeRoot, scopeBaseRef)
    = committed-section + in-progress-section
    where:
      committed-section: existing "Checkpoint context from commits
        in scope:" block, sourced from entire/checkpoints/v1
      in-progress-section: NEW "In-progress session context
        (uncommitted):" block, sourced from session state files
        (.git/entire-sessions/<id>.json) + the on-filesystem
        prompt.txt that lifecycle.go appends to every turn

Inclusion criteria for in-progress sessions (reviewSessionContext):
  - state.WorktreePath == current worktree (canonicalised through
    filepath.EvalSymlinks so /var vs /private/var on macOS matches)
  - state.BaseCommit == current HEAD (work since last commit only)
  - !state.FullyCondensed (still in flight)
  - state.Kind != KindAgentReview (don't include the review agent)

Per-session entry format mirrors the existing prompt-fallback path
(reviewPromptText), so the agent-facing output is consistent
whether the work is committed or in-progress:

  <sessionID[:8]> <AgentType> [(touched: N file(s))] prompt: <latest>

Reuses reviewPromptText for prompt rendering — no new truncation
logic, no new caps. If a session has no readable prompt.txt the
entry is skipped silently.

The compose layer (joinReviewContextSections) emits non-empty
sections joined by a blank line; ComposeReviewPrompt already
skips empty sections cleanly, so no plumbing change needed for
the "0 commits + 0 sessions" degenerate case.

Tests added:
- TestReviewSessionContext_IncludesActiveSessionWithLatestPrompt:
  unit-level, asserts the section text contains the session ID
  prefix, agent display name, and latest prompt.
- TestReviewSessionContext_SkipsSessionsOutsideScope: four-case
  exclusion check (FullyCondensed, WrongWorktree, WrongBaseCommit,
  KindAgentReview).
- TestReviewCommandSmoke_IncludesInProgressSessionContextInPrompt:
  end-to-end through the cobra command, asserts the in-progress
  block reaches the captured agent prompt. Would catch wiring
  regressions between reviewSessionContext, the deps bridge, and
  ComposeReviewPrompt that the unit tests alone cannot.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
